lessons.title: UDP, ports and multiplexing
lessons.summary: What the transport layer adds on top of IP, the 8-byte UDP header, how ports and 5-tuples route data to the right socket, and when UDP beats TCP (DNS, games, QUIC).
lessons.body:
IP delivers packets from one **host** to another. But a host can run many programs at once: a browser, a DNS resolver, an SSH session, a game. When a packet arrives, something has to decide which program gets it.

That is the transport layer's most basic job: **multiplexing** (many applications sharing one IP address on the way out) and **demultiplexing** (handing each arriving packet to the right application). The tool for it is the **port number**.

Two widely used Internet transports are TCP and UDP. Base **UDP** offers datagram boundaries, ports and a checksum, with few additional services. **TCP** adds a reliable, ordered byte stream with flow and congestion control. This module starts with UDP as a simple datagram transport; transport protocols need not all use the same multiplexing mechanism.

## Ports

A port is a 16-bit number, so 0 to 65,535. IANA splits the range into three bands:

| Range | Name | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| 0–1023 | System (well-known) | 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 443 HTTPS |
| 1024–49151 | User (registered) | 3306 MySQL, 5432 Postgres |
| 49152–65535 | Dynamic (ephemeral) | Client-side ports |

A server often **binds** to a known service port; discovery mechanisms can also advertise dynamically chosen ports. Port zero is reserved in the IANA registry, and asking a socket API to bind port zero typically requests automatic allocation. A client usually lets the OS pick a temporary **ephemeral port** for its end. Operating systems don't all follow the IANA range: Linux picks ephemeral ports from **32768–60999** by default (`net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range`), which spans 28,232 numbers before reserved ports, existing uses and configuration changes are considered.

On Unix, binding to ports below 1024 traditionally needs root (on Linux, typically `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, with the privileged-port threshold configurable per network namespace). That rule is a historical trust signal, not security.

## The UDP header

UDP ([RFC 768](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc768), 1980) is three pages long. Its header is 8 bytes:

```
 0      7 8     15 16    23 24    31
+--------+--------+--------+--------+
|   Source port   |    Dest port    |
+--------+--------+--------+--------+
|     Length      |    Checksum     |
+--------+--------+--------+--------+
|        data (payload) ...         |
+-----------------------------------+
```

- **Source port**: a reply-port hint when supplied; RFC 768 permits zero when unused. Application protocols can impose additional requirements.
- **Destination port**: which socket on the receiver gets this datagram.
- **Length**: header plus data, in bytes; at least 8 for an ordinary datagram. IPv6 jumbograms use the exception described below.
- **Checksum**: the 16-bit one's complement of the one's-complement sum over the header, the data and a **pseudo-header** of source IP, destination IP, protocol number and UDP length. Including addresses helps detect accidental misdelivery, but the checksum does not detect every error and provides no authentication.

The checksum is optional over IPv4 (a value of 0 means "not computed") and normally **required over IPv6**. RFC 6935/6936 permit narrowly constrained zero-checksum tunnel modes; ordinary IPv6 applications cannot simply disable it.

For ordinary UDP, the 16-bit length field bounds header plus payload at 65,535 bytes. IPv6 jumbograms are a specified exception (RFC 2675), using UDP length zero when required. Over IPv4, with a 20-byte IP header, the largest payload is 65,535 − 20 − 8 = **65,507 bytes**. An IP packet larger than the path MTU may be fragmented where allowed, rejected locally, or dropped with an ICMP error. Linux UDP normally uses PMTU discovery and can return `EMSGSIZE`. IPv6 routers do not fragment. Reassembly needs all fragments, so UDP applications should manage payload sizes using path and protocol constraints rather than assume one universal safe size.

> [!note] What UDP does not do
> Base UDP provides no handshake, acknowledgements, retransmission, ordering, flow control or congestion control. Datagrams may be lost, duplicated or reordered. Ordinary datagram socket calls preserve message boundaries; a too-small receive buffer can truncate a message and discard its remainder. A successful send is not proof of remote delivery.

RFC 9868 (October 2025) defines UDP transport options after the user-data area; it does not enlarge the base eight-byte header. This lesson describes ordinary datagrams without those options or socket segmentation/coalescing extensions.

## Demultiplexing: sockets and 5-tuples

An application talks to the transport layer through a **socket**. The kernel needs a rule for choosing which socket an arriving packet belongs to. UDP and TCP use different rules.

### UDP: match on the destination

An unconnected IPv4 UDP socket bound to `0.0.0.0:53` can receive datagrams addressed to port 53 across local IPv4 addresses. Filtering, competing specific/reuse bindings, multicast membership and implementation rules can affect delivery. A DNS server can use one bound UDP socket for requests from many different client endpoints, reading each sender's address from `recvfrom()`.

```python
import socket

s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,
                  socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 9999))
while True:
    data, addr = s.recvfrom(2048)
    s.sendto(data.upper(), addr)
```

The echo example binds loopback and truncates received datagrams above 2,048 bytes; it is a small demonstration, not a production service.

Calling `connect()` on a UDP socket establishes a default peer and normally restricts received datagrams to it. It performs no UDP handshake; route lookup or neighbour resolution and socket error handling can still occur. API details, including whether explicit sends to other destinations are permitted, vary.

### TCP: match on the full 5-tuple

A TCP connection is identified by its **5-tuple**:

```
(protocol, src IP, src port,
           dst IP, dst port)
```

A web server listening on port 443 has one listening socket, plus one **accepted socket per TCP connection**. Two separate connections from one client address can differ in source port; browser tabs can also share pooled connections:

```
TCP 198.51.100.7:51000 -> 203.0.113.5:443
TCP 198.51.100.7:51001 -> 203.0.113.5:443
```

Both arrive at the same server port, but they differ in one field, so they are different connections. This is why a server can handle hundreds of thousands of connections on a single port: capacity depends on resources such as memory, file descriptors, CPU and distinct connection tuples; one server port does not impose a 65,535-connection total limit.

> [!example] Ephemeral port exhaustion
> A client connects repeatedly to one backend, `10.0.0.5:5432`. Four of the five fields are fixed; only the source port varies. With Linux's default range, with a single fixed source address and automatic allocation confined to that range, at most 28,232 distinct local ports are available before other reservations and constraints. TIME_WAIT can further restrict tuple reuse (lesson 2). Proxies hit this; fixes are connection pooling, extra source IPs, or more backend IPs.

## Why would anyone choose UDP?

TCP gives you reliability and ordering, but you pay in **latency** (a normal new-connection handshake and possible waits for retransmissions; extensions and connection reuse change this cost) and **control** (the kernel decides when to send and what to wait for). UDP is right when one of those costs is unacceptable.

### DNS: one question, one answer

A DNS lookup is usually a single small query and a single small response. With UDP the whole exchange takes **one round trip**. A fresh ordinary TCP connection adds a handshake; an already open connection can be reused, and TCP Fast Open can alter setup timing. Total resolution latency also includes DNS processing and any upstream queries.

Reliability is handled by the application: if no reply arrives within a timeout, the resolver asks again or tries another server. If a response is too big for UDP, the server sets the **TC (truncated)** flag and the client retries over TCP. EDNS(0) allows UDP responses bigger than the original 512-byte limit; DNS Flag Day 2020 recommended a 1,232-byte UDP payload limit (IPv6 minimum MTU 1,280 minus 40-byte base IPv6 and 8-byte UDP headers). This reduces fragmentation risk under those assumptions rather than proving every path can carry it.

### Real-time games and voice: stale data is useless

Consider a game sending independent full-state position snapshots at 60 Hz, about 16.7 ms apart. A new snapshot can supersede a lost one; delta updates and important game events can have different reliability requirements. TCP would **hold back** every later update until the lost one was retransmitted, delaying delivery of later bytes until the gap is repaired. The delay depends on detection, retransmission and buffering; the whole game loop need not freeze. That is **head-of-line blocking**, and independent deadline-sensitive updates can prefer skipping stale data to waiting for that gap.

Voice and video calls (RTP over UDP) work the same way: a late frame may be concealed or discarded, but timely retransmission and forward error correction can also help. RFC 4588 specifies RTP retransmission; media deadlines determine its usefulness.

### QUIC: build your own transport

QUIC ([RFC 9000](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)), the transport under HTTP/3, uses UDP; HTTP/3 commonly uses **port 443**, but QUIC is not restricted to that port. QUIC provides its own loss recovery, stream reliability, congestion control and protected transport, and can be implemented in user space. UDP is used not because QUIC wants unreliability, but because using existing UDP socket support can ease endpoint and middlebox deployment. UDP is neither the only permitted non-TCP transport nor guaranteed to pass every path. Lesson 6 covers why.

### Others

Examples using UDP include DHCPv4 initial discovery, conventional NTP/SNMP exchanges, UDP syslog, multicast media and WireGuard. Several of these application families also define other transports; “syslog” alone does not imply UDP.

## Pitfalls of UDP

- **You own congestion control.** UDP will happily send faster than the network can carry, hurting everyone. [RFC 8085](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8085) requires applications to account for congestion and describes suitable control or rate-limiting behaviour for different traffic patterns; low-volume applications are not universally exempt.
- **Amplification attacks.** With no handshake, an attacker can spoof a victim's source address and send small queries to open servers that reply with much bigger responses. Cloudflare documented large amplification from exposed Memcached UDP services in 2018. Amplification depends on the request, stored response and counting of protocol overhead; the attack does not follow merely from choosing UDP.
- **NAT and firewalls.** Idle mapping lifetimes vary. RFC 4787 specifies a normal minimum of two minutes, with a defined exception for some well-known destination ports; actual equipment may differ. Applications needing inbound reachability must account for the relevant timeout and keepalive policy. Some corporate networks block UDP outright, so clients supporting HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 can fall back to TCP; a QUIC-only application has no automatic TCP fallback.
- **Fragmentation.** Oversized datagrams may fail locally or require permitted fragmentation. Fragment loss or filtering can prevent reassembly; UDP does not retransmit the missing data.

## Key takeaways
- The transport layer multiplexes many applications onto one IP address using 16-bit port numbers.
- UDP adds only ports, a length and a checksum (8 bytes) to IP. Datagrams keep their boundaries but may be lost, duplicated or reordered.
- Unconnected UDP delivery is primarily selected by local endpoint, while connected sockets can also match the peer; TCP connections are identified by the full 5-tuple, so one server port can serve many clients.
- With one fixed source address and automatic allocation confined to a range, simultaneous connections to one destination are limited by that source-port pool (28,232 numbers in the documented default Linux allocation range, before other constraints).
- Choose UDP when a handshake or head-of-line blocking costs more than the reliability is worth: DNS, real-time media and games, and protocols like QUIC that build their own transport.
- With UDP you take on congestion control, amplification risk and NAT timeouts yourself.

questions.prompt: How big is the UDP header?

options.text: 20 bytes
options.explanation: 20 bytes is the minimum size of the IPv4 header and of the TCP header, not UDP. UDP is deliberately tiny.

options.text: 8 bytes
options.explanation: Correct. Four 16-bit fields: source port, destination port, length and checksum.

options.text: 4 bytes
options.explanation: That would only fit the two port numbers. UDP also carries a length and a checksum.

options.text: It varies with options
options.explanation: The base UDP header remains eight bytes. RFC 9868 defines UDP options in a surplus area after user data, rather than making that base header variable length.

questions.workedExample:
UDP's header is four fields of 16 bits each:

```
src port   16 bits
dst port   16 bits
length     16 bits
checksum   16 bits
---------------------
total      64 bits = 8 bytes
```

Compare TCP's minimum of 20 bytes, which has to carry sequence numbers, acknowledgement numbers, flags and a window. UDP needs none of those because it promises none of those services.

questions.prompt: Over IPv4 with a 20-byte IP header (no options), what is the largest payload a single UDP datagram can carry?

options.text: 65,535 bytes
options.explanation: 65,535 is the maximum of the 16-bit length field, but that value counts the 8-byte UDP header, and the IPv4 total-length field also has to fit the IP header.

options.text: 1,472 bytes
options.explanation: That is the largest payload that avoids fragmentation on a 1,500-byte Ethernet MTU (1,500 − 20 − 8). It is a practical limit, not the protocol maximum.

options.text: 65,527 bytes
options.explanation: This subtracts the UDP header from 65,535 but forgets that the IPv4 total-length field (also 16 bits) must include the 20-byte IP header.

options.text: 65,507 bytes
options.explanation: Correct. The IPv4 total length is at most 65,535 bytes; subtract 20 for the IP header and 8 for the UDP header.

questions.workedExample:
1. IPv4 total length is at most 65,535 bytes.
2. Subtract the specified 20-byte IPv4 header and eight-byte UDP header: 65,507 payload bytes.
3. With fragmentation permitted, equal 20-byte fragment headers and MTU 1,500, the 65,515-byte IP payload needs 45 fragments (44 × 1,480 + 395). All fragments are needed for reassembly.
4. Otherwise sending may fail locally or on the path. With those same headers and MTU, 1,472 UDP payload bytes fit without fragmentation; other paths and encapsulation have different limits.

questions.prompt: Which facilities does base UDP provide, without higher-level reliability protocols? Select all that apply.

options.text: Delivery to the right application via port numbers
options.explanation: Correct. UDP uses port fields to support application demultiplexing; not every possible transport protocol must use UDP-style ports.

options.text: Detection of corrupted datagrams via a checksum
options.explanation: Correct. When enabled and verified, the checksum detects some corruption, including in the pseudo-header. It does not detect all errors or authenticate the sender, and IPv4 permits omission.

options.text: Retransmission of lost datagrams
options.explanation: UDP never retransmits. If an application needs reliability (as DNS resolvers do), it must implement timeouts and retries itself.

options.text: Preservation of message boundaries
options.explanation: Correct for ordinary UDP socket use. Received datagrams remain separate; too-small buffers can truncate a datagram, and successful sending does not guarantee delivery.

options.text: In-order delivery
options.explanation: Base UDP does not specify ordered delivery or receive-side resequencing. Applications can add their own sequence information and ordering policy.

questions.workedExample: Base UDP defines source/destination ports, a datagram length and a checksum. These support demultiplexing, message boundaries and limited error detection. It does not define ordered delivery or automatic loss recovery. Protocol guarantees follow from the specification and state machine, not merely from whether a similarly named header field exists.

questions.prompt:
On localhost, a UDP client runs:

```python
s.sendto(b"a" * 100, srv)
s.sendto(b"b" * 200, srv)
s.sendto(b"c" * 300, srv)
```

The server loops on `data, _ = s.recvfrom(2048)` and prints `len(data)`. Assuming ordinary datagram socket calls, no loss, duplication or reordering, what does it print?

options.explanation: That is what a TCP receiver might see, since TCP is a byte stream and can merge writes. UDP never merges datagrams.

options.text: `100`, `200`, `300` on separate lines
options.explanation: Correct. UDP preserves message boundaries: three `sendto()` calls produce three datagrams, and each `recvfrom()` returns exactly one.

options.text: `2048` three times
options.explanation: The 2048 is the buffer size, the maximum the call will return. `recvfrom` returns the actual datagram length.

options.text: It depends on how the kernel chooses to split the data
options.explanation: Ordinary UDP sockets preserve datagram boundaries. Here the buffer is large enough; smaller receive buffers can truncate a message rather than return it whole.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each `sendto()` builds one UDP datagram with its own length field: 100, 200, 300 bytes of payload.
2. The receiver's kernel queues each datagram as a separate unit.
3. Each `recvfrom(2048)` dequeues one datagram. The buffer is big enough, so nothing is truncated.
4. Output:

```
100
200
300
```

Two caveats: over a real network the order could change or one could vanish; and if the buffer were smaller than a datagram (say `recvfrom(50)`), the excess would be **discarded**, not saved for the next call.

questions.prompt: A proxy uses one source IP and automatic source ports restricted to 32768–60999, all available initially. It repeatedly connects to one backend, 10.0.0.5:5432. Assume negligible active connection duration, exactly 60 seconds of tuple unavailability after closure, no early reuse and no other bottleneck. What approximate sustained rate does this model allow?

options.text: About 65,000 per second
options.explanation: This assumes all 65,536 port numbers are usable and each is freed instantly. Only the ephemeral range is used, and each port is held for 60 s.

options.text: About 28,000 per second
options.explanation: 28,232 is the number of ports, but each is unavailable for 60 seconds after use, so they can't all be reused every second.

options.text: About 470 per second
options.explanation: Correct. 28,232 ports ÷ 60 seconds ≈ 470 new connections per second to that one destination.

options.text: Unlimited, because the 5-tuple includes the destination
options.explanation: The destination is fixed here (one IP, one port), as are protocol and source IP. Only the source port varies, so it is the bottleneck.

questions.workedExample:
1. Four of the five tuple fields are fixed: TCP, the proxy's IP, `10.0.0.5`, port 5432. Only the **source port** can vary.
2. Ports available: 60999 − 32768 + 1 = **28,232**.
3. Each one is unusable for 60 seconds after its connection closes.
4. Under the stated model, steady-state rate = ports ÷ hold time:

```
28,232 / 60 s ≈ 470 conn/s
```

Fixes: reuse connections (a pool), add backend IPs or source IPs (can add tuple capacity, subject to allocation and bind behaviour), or widen the port range.

questions.prompt: An HTTPS service accepts 100,000 simultaneous TCP connections on one server IP and local port 443. How many distinct local TCP port numbers do those accepted sockets use?

options.text: 100,000, one per client
options.explanation: The server does not allocate a new port per client. Each accepted connection gets a new socket, but it shares the listening port.

options.text: At most 65,535, so it cannot have 100,000 clients
options.explanation: This confuses the port space with the connection space. Connections are identified by 5-tuples, of which there are vastly more than 65,535.

options.text: About 28,000, the size of the ephemeral range
options.explanation: These accepted sockets retain the listener’s local port. The initiating endpoint may choose an ephemeral source port or explicitly bind one.

options.text: One: port 443, with connections told apart by the client's IP and port
options.explanation: Correct. All connections have destination port 443; the kernel demultiplexes them by the full 5-tuple, in which the client's address and port differ.

questions.workedExample:
1. Every client connects to `server_ip:443`.
2. On the server, `accept()` returns a new socket for each connection, but that socket's local address is still `server_ip:443`.
3. The kernel tells them apart by the 5-tuple:

```
(TCP, c1_ip, c1_port, srv, 443)
(TCP, c2_ip, c2_port, srv, 443)
...
```

4. So the server uses one port. Practical limits include memory, file descriptors, CPU and connection-tuple availability; this question specifies a service using just one local port.

questions.prompt: Which requirements can motivate an application to use ordinary UDP datagrams with application-specific control instead of one TCP byte stream? This compares base transports, not reliable protocols such as QUIC built above UDP. Select all that apply.

options.text: Independent full-state game snapshots where superseded updates should not block newer ones
options.explanation: Correct. The application can discard stale snapshots and avoid TCP byte-stream head-of-line blocking. Important events or delta-dependent state may require separate reliability.

options.text: A software download whose only stated requirement is reliable delivery of every file byte
options.explanation: That requirement alone does not motivate replacing TCP with base UDP. A higher-level reliable protocol such as QUIC can also carry downloads; this is not a claim that files cannot use UDP-based transports.

options.text: A small DNS request/reply where avoiding a fresh transport handshake is useful
options.explanation: Correct. UDP can carry the small exchange without a transport handshake; DNS still needs retries, validation and TCP support where required. Existing TCP connections can be reused.

options.text: Deadline-sensitive voice packets for which later packets should not wait for expired ones
options.explanation: Correct. Media-specific loss recovery can respect playback deadlines. Concealment, FEC or timely retransmission can all be useful; retransmission is not universally pointless.

options.text: A payment API whose only stated requirement is that the transaction must not be lost
options.explanation: Base UDP adds no delivery guarantee. TCP or QUIC can carry reliable data, but neither alone guarantees durable payment processing: acknowledgements, retries and idempotency belong at the application layer.

questions.workedExample: Select the requirements that benefit from independent datagrams or no fresh transport handshake: snapshots, a small DNS exchange and deadline-sensitive voice. A file’s completeness requirement or a payment’s durability requirement alone does not motivate bare UDP. Reliable transports built over UDP remain valid options, and application correctness is separate from byte delivery.

questions.prompt: A resolver sends a DNS query over UDP. The answer is too large for the UDP size the server is willing to send. What happens in standard DNS?

options.text: The server sends a truncated reply with the TC flag set, and the client retries the query over TCP
options.explanation: Correct for this standard truncation/retry path. DNS-over-TCP supports larger messages, but still uses a two-byte message-length field; it is not unlimited.

options.text: The server fragments the response into several UDP datagrams and the client reassembles them
options.explanation: DNS has no application-level reassembly of UDP replies. IP fragmentation can occur, but it is exactly what DNS tries to avoid.

options.text: The server silently drops the query
options.explanation: The server does answer: it marks the reply as truncated so the client knows to retry.

options.text: UDP automatically switches to TCP mode
options.explanation: UDP has no such mode. The switch to TCP is done by the DNS client, prompted by the TC flag.

questions.workedExample:
1. Original UDP DNS used a 512-byte limit; EDNS lets a requester advertise a larger UDP payload size.
2. DNS Flag Day 2020 recommended 1,232 bytes to reduce fragmentation risk under IPv6 minimum-MTU/header assumptions.
3. A truncated response sets TC; the resolver can retry using TCP as specified by DNS handling rules.
4. A new TCP connection adds handshake cost; a reusable connection changes that timing. DNS-over-TCP messages still have a 65,535-byte length-field limit.

questions.prompt: An attacker controls machines that can send 100 Mbit/s of spoofed UDP queries, with the source address set to a victim's IP, to open servers whose replies are 50 times bigger than the queries. Why does this work, and how much traffic hits the victim? Assume the factor includes the same overhead basis as the 100 Mbit/s figure, and all queries/replies are delivered without rate limiting or capacity constraints.

options.text: It works because UDP has no checksum; about 100 Mbit/s
options.explanation: UDP does have a checksum, and it is irrelevant here. The trick is the spoofed source, and the traffic is multiplied.

options.text: It works because TCP SYN cookies are disabled; about 5 Gbit/s
options.explanation: SYN cookies are a TCP defence and have nothing to do with UDP. The figure is right but the mechanism is wrong.

options.text: It can't work: the replies go back to the attacker's machines
options.explanation: With a spoofed source address, the replies go to whatever address is in the source field: the victim.

options.text: It works because UDP has no handshake, so servers reply to a forged address; about 5 Gbit/s
options.explanation: Correct under the assumptions. UDP itself performs no return-routability handshake, and these servers respond without additional validation: 100 Mbit/s × 50 = 5 Gbit/s.

questions.workedExample:
1. The scenario explicitly allows spoofed requests through source-address filters.
2. These servers send responses to the claimed source without further validation.
3. With consistent size accounting and no limiting bottleneck, 100 Mbit/s × 50 = 5 Gbit/s at the victim.
4. Source validation, response limits and protocol-level address validation can reduce this risk. TCP’s handshake changes the attack surface but does not make all TCP reflection or denial-of-service attacks impossible.

questions.prompt: A game sends 60 small position updates per second to the server over **TCP**. RTT is 100 ms. One segment carrying an update is lost. What does the server's game loop experience?

options.text: It misses that one update and carries on with the next one 16 ms later
options.explanation: TCP does not skip missing stream bytes to expose later ones. UDP-based independent snapshots can avoid that stream-ordering constraint, subject to loss and scheduling.

options.text: Nothing at all, because TCP retransmits transparently
options.explanation: The retransmission is transparent to correctness, not to timing. The delay it causes is the whole problem.

options.text: Later bytes on that TCP stream wait for the missing bytes; after recovery, several buffered updates may become readable
options.explanation: Correct. TCP exposes an ordered byte stream. The question’s RTT does not specify an exact stall duration or imply the application’s whole game loop freezes.

options.text: The TCP connection is reset
options.explanation: One lost segment does not by itself instruct TCP to reset. Recovery is normally attempted; repeated failure can eventually reach an implementation or application timeout.

questions.workedExample:
1. Later stream bytes can arrive out of order and be buffered.
2. TCP cannot expose them as contiguous application data until the earlier gap is filled.
3. Detection and recovery time depend on ACKs, timers, the loss position and implementation. RTT alone provides no exact pause duration.
4. At 60 Hz, six update intervals span 100 ms, but that arithmetic is only an illustration, not a guaranteed six-update stall.
5. An application can continue local prediction or other work while waiting.

questions.prompt: Why does QUIC run on top of UDP rather than as a brand-new IP protocol alongside TCP and UDP? Select all that apply.

options.text: Using existing UDP support can ease traversal of middleboxes compared with introducing a new IP protocol number
options.explanation: Correct. Some devices filter unknown protocols or lack suitable translation support. Devices can support other transports too, and UDP can itself be blocked.

options.text: UDP lets QUIC be implemented in an application or library in user space, without waiting for OS kernels to be updated
options.explanation: Correct. Existing UDP socket interfaces allow QUIC implementations in application libraries; operating-system policy and network access still apply.

options.text: UDP provides the reliability QUIC needs, so QUIC doesn't have to implement it
options.explanation: UDP provides no reliability. QUIC implements acknowledgements, retransmission and congestion control itself.

options.text: UDP's checksum replaces the need for encryption
options.explanation: The checksum is not cryptographic authentication. QUIC uses TLS 1.3 for its handshake and derives keys for packet protection; a checksum does not replace that.

questions.workedExample:
1. Reusing UDP allows implementations to use existing endpoint socket APIs and network support.
2. This can reduce the deployment changes required by a new IP protocol.
3. It does not make UDP universally reachable or restrict QUIC to user-space implementations.
4. QUIC supplies its own loss recovery, stream ordering, congestion control and packet protection above UDP.

lessons.title: TCP connection management
lessons.summary: The three-way handshake with real sequence numbers, SYN floods and SYN cookies, the four-way close, why TIME_WAIT lasts 2×MSL, the TCP state machine and when connections are reset.
lessons.body:
TCP offers a **reliable, ordered byte stream** between two endpoints. Normal establishment synchronises sequence spaces and checks bidirectional reachability; this is not cryptographic peer authentication. Data can accompany handshake segments, and extensions such as TCP Fast Open can allow early application delivery. Graceful closure acknowledges the byte stream in each direction, not application processing or durable storage of those bytes. That bookkeeping is **connection management**.

The rules come from RFC 793 (1981), now consolidated in [RFC 9293](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293) (2022).

## The TCP header, briefly

The fields that matter for connection management:

- **Sequence number** (32 bits): the first sequence-space position in the segment; a SYN occupies its own position before any data.
- **Acknowledgement number** (32 bits): the next byte the sender expects to receive. Only valid when the ACK flag is set.
- **Flags**: `SYN` (synchronise sequence numbers), `ACK`, `FIN` (no more data from me), `RST` (abort), plus `PSH`, `URG`, `ECE`, `CWR`.
- **Window** (16 bits): flow control (lesson 4).
- **Options**: MSS, window scale, SACK-permitted, timestamps. MSS, window scale and SACK permission are exchanged on SYN segments. Negotiated timestamps accompany later segments, and SACK blocks can appear on later ACKs.

The header is 20 bytes without options and at most 60 with them.

## The three-way handshake

Each side picks an **initial sequence number** (ISN). The handshake exchanges and acknowledges both:

```
Client                       Server
  |  SYN seq=1000              |
  |--------------------------->|
  |                            |
  |  SYN+ACK seq=5000 ack=1001 |
  |<---------------------------|
  |                            |
  |  ACK seq=1001 ack=5001     |
  |--------------------------->|
  |  (data can now flow)       |
```

Two rules make the numbers work:

1. **SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number**, independently of any data carried in the same segment. That is why the server acknowledges 1001, not 1000.
2. The cumulative ACK identifies the next expected sequence-space position in that direction, modulo 2^32. It acknowledges contiguous received stream data/control positions, not successful application processing.

So the client's first data byte will be numbered 1001, and the server's 5001. The final ACK may carry data itself; clients often send the HTTP request or TLS ClientHello right behind it.

### Why three messages, not two?

Each side must learn that the **other** side received its ISN. The client's SYN is acknowledged by the server's SYN+ACK; the server's SYN is acknowledged by the client's final ACK. Two messages would leave the server not knowing whether its ISN arrived.

There is also the **old duplicate** problem. A SYN delayed in the network from a long-dead attempt could arrive at the server. With three messages, the server's SYN+ACK reaches a client that is not expecting it, and the client replies with RST. If that response arrives, the server abandons the stale attempt. With no reply, it can retain half-open state until timeout; the handshake is not a defence against every spoof or replay scenario.

### Why random ISNs?

If ISNs were predictable (say, always 0), two problems arise:

- **Stale segments**: a delayed segment from a previous connection with the same 5-tuple could fall inside the new connection's sequence space and be accepted as data.
- **Spoofing**: an off-path attacker who can guess the server's ISN can forge the final ACK and inject data while pretending to be another IP. Predictable sequence numbers have historically enabled off-path spoofing; reachability and other validation assumptions also matter.

[RFC 6528](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6528), incorporated into RFC 9293, describes a clock component plus a keyed function of endpoint addresses/ports. RFC 9293 discusses an approximately 4 µs clock; actual implementations can differ. The construction aims to make new ISNs hard for an off-path attacker to predict while separating connection incarnations.

## SYN floods and SYN cookies

When a server receives a SYN, normal stateful Linux processing creates **request-socket** state associated with the listener and sends SYN+ACK. Exact memory use depends on kernel/configuration. It retransmits the SYN+ACK if no ACK comes back: the Linux documentation retrieved here specifies five SYN+ACK retries by default, with a one-second initial timeout and a final timeout near 63 seconds. This is a documented default, not a universal timing guarantee.

A **SYN flood** attempts to exhaust connection-establishment resources with SYN traffic, often using spoofed addresses. The final ACKs never arrive, the SYN queue fills with half-open entries, and real clients' SYNs are dropped. The attacker needs no completed connections and can hide behind random sources.

### SYN cookies

A **SYN cookie** avoids retaining an ordinary per-attempt half-open entry: encode enough information in the server's sequence-number construction to validate a returning ACK and reconstruct connection state. Secret keys and other shared server state still exist, and processing consumes CPU and bandwidth.

A conceptual flow is:

```
SYN + endpoint tuple
        |
        v
secret + time + supported option state
        |
        v
cookie sequence number -> SYN+ACK
        |
client returns ACK acknowledging cookie
        |
validate freshness/authenticator
        |
create established-connection state
```

The exact encoding is implementation-specific. Recovering the acknowledged server sequence number uses `ack - 1` modulo 2^32, followed by the implementation's validation rules. An off-path attacker that cannot observe the SYN+ACK must guess a valid value; finite cookie authenticators do not make guessing mathematically impossible.

Costs:

- Limited cookie space constrains the amount of MSS/option state encoded; the set of supported MSS values depends on the implementation.
- Option support can be reduced; implementations may encode extra state in negotiated timestamp fields. Behaviour varies by version and client options.
- Without per-attempt timer state, there is no autonomous SYN+ACK retransmission timer for that attempt. A retransmitted client SYN can elicit another SYN+ACK.

Linux has its own cookie construction. Its documented default, `net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1`, sends cookies **only when the SYN queue overflows**, when the kernel is built with SYN-cookie support; value 2 requests unconditional generation. Cookies do not remedy every overload or network-capacity problem. Large providers also filter floods upstream, before they reach servers.

## Closing: the four-way exchange

TCP connections are **full duplex**, so each direction is closed separately. Either side sends FIN to say "I have no more data". The other side acknowledges it, may keep sending, and later sends its own FIN.

```
A (active close)        B (passive)
ESTABLISHED             ESTABLISHED
  | FIN seq=8000          |
  |---------------------->| CLOSE_WAIT
FIN_WAIT_1                |
  |          ACK ack=8001 |
  |<----------------------|
FIN_WAIT_2                |
  |   (B may send more)   |
  |          FIN seq=9000 |
  |<----------------------| LAST_ACK
TIME_WAIT                 |
  | ACK ack=9001          |
  |---------------------->| CLOSED
(wait 2 x MSL)
CLOSED
```

B often combines its ACK and FIN into one segment, giving three segments in total. A **half-close** (`shutdown(SHUT_WR)` on A) sends a FIN but keeps receiving; that is how a client can say "that's my whole request" and still read the response.

## TIME_WAIT and 2×MSL

In the ordinary sequential graceful close above, the active closer ends in **TIME_WAIT**, and stays there for twice the **maximum segment lifetime** (MSL), the longest a segment is assumed to survive in the network.

Simultaneous close can put both endpoints in TIME_WAIT; aborts and special reuse cases follow different rules. Two purposes of TIME_WAIT are:

1. **A retransmitted FIN may need another ACK.** Keeping connection state lets the endpoint acknowledge a repeated FIN if the peer missed the final ACK. The TIME_WAIT timer can restart when the FIN is received again. MSL is a segment-lifetime assumption, not the peer's retransmission timeout, so adding two presumed network delays is not a proof of the retransmission schedule.
2. **Old duplicates must expire.** Retaining the connection incarnation for the specified interval reduces confusion if the same endpoint tuple is reused. The guarantee relies on the MSL/sequence-number assumptions; TCP also specifies constrained early-reuse cases.

RFC 793 suggested an MSL of 2 minutes (so 4 minutes of TIME_WAIT). Linux v6.12 defines its ordinary TIME_WAIT interval as **60 seconds**; reuse, retransmitted segments and resource handling can affect an observed entry’s lifetime.

### TIME_WAIT in production

TIME_WAIT is cheap (Linux keeps a small, stripped-down structure), but it constrains reuse of the **5-tuple** under the implementation’s rules:

- A client or proxy making many short connections to **one** backend can exhaust ephemeral ports (lesson 1).
- A server that actively closes connections accumulates TIME_WAIT entries, but on a single listening port a large connection count is still possible because peers have distinct tuples. Memory, churn and reuse patterns can nevertheless matter.

Possible approaches, chosen for the application and deployment:

1. **Reuse connections**: HTTP keep-alive, connection pools.
2. Changing which endpoint performs the sequential active close moves TIME_WAIT ownership; it does not create spare ports or solve the problem universally.
3. `net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse`: enables reuse subject to Linux’s protocol-safety checks; timestamps are not a cryptographic proof. The retrieved Linux documentation lists default 2 (loopback only) and a separate reuse delay. Do not treat this as a universal replacement for pooling.

> [!warning] Never use tcp_tw_recycle
> The old `tcp_tw_recycle` option dropped SYNs whose timestamps went backwards, which broke clients behind NAT whose clocks differ. It was removed in Linux 4.12. Advice to enable it is outdated.

## The state machine

RFC 9293 defines 11 states. The table below abbreviates successful ordinary events. Sequence/ACK validity, acceptable in-order FIN processing, queued data, duplicate packets, reset/error paths and API details are omitted:

| From | Event | To |
|---|---|---|
| CLOSED | `listen()` | LISTEN |
| CLOSED | `connect()`, send SYN | SYN_SENT |
| LISTEN | recv SYN, send SYN+ACK | SYN_RCVD |
| SYN_SENT | recv SYN+ACK, send ACK | ESTABLISHED |
| SYN_RCVD | recv ACK | ESTABLISHED |
| ESTABLISHED | `close()`, send FIN | FIN_WAIT_1 |
| ESTABLISHED | recv FIN, send ACK | CLOSE_WAIT |
| FIN_WAIT_1 | own FIN acknowledged; no peer FIN processed | FIN_WAIT_2 |
| FIN_WAIT_1 | peer FIN processed; own FIN not acknowledged | CLOSING |
| FIN_WAIT_1 | peer FIN processed and own FIN acknowledged | TIME_WAIT |
| FIN_WAIT_2 | recv FIN, send ACK | TIME_WAIT |
| CLOSING | own FIN acknowledged | TIME_WAIT |
| CLOSE_WAIT | `close()`, send FIN | LAST_ACK |
| LAST_ACK | own FIN acknowledged | CLOSED |
| TIME_WAIT | 2×MSL timer | CLOSED |

CLOSING happens when both sides send FIN before receiving the other’s FIN and then process the crossing FINs before ACKs of their own FINs (a **simultaneous close**). Both then go through TIME_WAIT.

You can see live states with `ss -tan`:

```
$ ss -Htan state close-wait | wc -l
```

> [!tip] Investigate persistent CLOSE_WAIT growth
> CLOSE_WAIT means a peer FIN has been processed and the local send direction remains open. The application may legitimately still be preparing a response. Persistent unexplained growth can indicate leaked sockets or stalled handlers; use process-level descriptor and application evidence before diagnosing a leak. `shutdown(SHUT_WR)` or closing the final relevant descriptor can initiate the local FIN; process exit or an abort can also change the state.

## RST: aborting a connection

An accepted, valid RST tells the peer "this connection does not exist, or is being torn down now". A reset is not itself acknowledged and normally aborts the connection without a graceful FIN/TIME_WAIT sequence. Invalid RSTs can be ignored or challenged, and existing TIME_WAIT handling has additional rules. Common causes:

- **SYN to a port nobody listens on**: normal unfiltered TCP processing replies with RST, which the client can report as `ECONNREFUSED` ("connection refused"). If a firewall silently drops the SYN instead, the client sees a timeout.
- **Segment for an unknown connection**: for example after a server reboots and forgets its connections. The client can receive a reset once traffic reaches the rebooted peer; the exact API error depends on state and operations.
- **Abortive close**: on Linux, enabled `SO_LINGER` with a timeout of 0, then `close()`, sends RST instead of FIN. Load balancers sometimes do this to avoid TIME_WAIT.
- **Closing with unread data**: Linux sends RST if the application closes a socket while received data sits unread in its buffer, because that data will never be delivered.
- **Middleboxes**: firewalls and NATs that time out an idle connection may reset it.

A forged valid RST can abort a connection. For synchronized connections, [RFC 5961](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5961) specifies accepting an RST only when its sequence number exactly matches the next expected sequence-space position. Opening-state reset validation follows separate rules. If it is merely in the window, the stack sends a **challenge ACK** instead, which can elicit a correctly sequenced reset from a peer that has lost the connection. This is a robustness check, not cryptographic authentication; rate limits and side channels affect practical attack resistance.

## Key takeaways
- The three-way handshake exchanges and acknowledges both initial sequence numbers; SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number.
- ISNs are randomised to reject stale segments and resist spoofed injection.
- SYN floods can exhaust establishment resources; SYN cookies avoid an ordinary per-attempt half-open entry while retaining shared state and consuming processing resources. Valid cookie acknowledgements are a return-path check, not cryptographic client identity.
- Each direction of an ordinary graceful close uses its own FIN. In the sequential close model, the active closer ends in TIME_WAIT for 2×MSL (60 s in Linux v6.12) to ACK a retransmitted FIN and let old duplicates expire.
- TIME_WAIT is normal; unexplained CLOSE_WAIT growth warrants investigation of application lifecycle and descriptor ownership.
- An accepted valid RST normally aborts the connection; invalid resets may be ignored or challenged. Refused attempts, unknown connections and some close paths can generate resets.

The sequence number is right, but ack=5000 would claim the server's SYN hasn't been received yet. The ACK names the next byte expected, which is 5001.
Correct. The client's SYN consumed 1000, so it continues at 1001. The server's SYN consumed 5000, so the client acknowledges with 5001, meaning 'send me byte 5001 next'.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each direction has its own sequence space. The client's ISN is 1000; the server's is 5000.
2. **A SYN consumes one sequence number**, even with no data. So the client's SYN occupies number 1000, and the client's next number is **1001**. That matches the server's `ack=1001`.
3. The server's SYN occupies 5000. The client has received it, so the next server byte it wants is **5001**.
4. The final segment is therefore:

```
ACK seq=1001 ack=5001
```

If the client puts data in this segment (say a TLS ClientHello), the first data byte is numbered 1001.

questions.workedExample:

3. The browser closes and sends its FIN (LAST_ACK).

questions.prompt: Why does the active closer wait in TIME_WAIT for 2×MSL instead of going straight to CLOSED? Select all that apply.

options.text: If its final ACK is lost, the peer will retransmit its FIN, and someone must be there to ACK it again
options.explanation: Correct. Retained state allows another ACK of a repeated FIN. MSL is not a retransmission timer, and exact reset/error outcomes after state deletion depend on processing.

options.text: To let delayed segments from this connection expire before a new connection reuses the same 5-tuple
options.explanation: Correct. A stray old segment with the same 5-tuple could otherwise fall inside the new connection's window and be accepted as data.

options.text: To give the application time to read any data still in the receive buffer
options.explanation: TIME_WAIT is not an application read-grace mechanism. An application can initiate a half-close with shutdown while retaining a descriptor, so it need not already have discarded every socket reference.

options.text: To wait for the congestion window to drain before the port is reused
options.explanation: The congestion window limits outstanding transmitted data; TIME_WAIT is not a wait for that numeric limit to “drain”.

options.text: Because the passive closer is still sending data and needs it acknowledged
options.explanation: By the time the active closer is in TIME_WAIT, the passive closer has sent its FIN, so it has no more data to send.

questions.workedExample:
1. If the peer missed the final ACK, retained state can acknowledge a retransmitted FIN; receiving the FIN can restart the TIME_WAIT timer.
2. The specified waiting interval also protects later connection incarnations from old duplicates under the assumed maximum segment lifetime.
3. The peer’s retransmission timeout is separate from MSL, so “one MSL until an ACK vanishes plus one for the FIN” is not a valid timer derivation.
4. Standards and implementations define constrained reuse cases; this is not an unconditional prohibition on any earlier tuple reuse.

questions.prompt: A Python service approaches its descriptor limit. Process-level inspection confirms thousands of its sockets remain in CLOSE_WAIT long after their handlers have finished, with no intended half-close work. What should be investigated first?

options.text: TIME_WAIT is lasting too long; lower the TIME_WAIT timeout
options.explanation: The evidence concerns descriptors retained by this process in CLOSE_WAIT. Normal TIME_WAIT state after final descriptor closure does not retain those application descriptors.

options.text: The service doesn't close sockets after the peer closes, for example on an error path
options.explanation: Correct. Completed handlers retaining these sockets suggest a lifecycle/ownership leak. CLOSE_WAIT alone can also be legitimate while an application finishes sending, but the prompt excludes that case.

options.text: A SYN flood is filling the SYN queue
options.explanation: A SYN flood targets establishment resources; the observed sockets have progressed to peer-FIN processing and are retained by completed handlers.

options.text: The network is dropping the final ACKs of the handshake
options.explanation: Missing establishment ACKs do not explain these already retained CLOSE_WAIT sockets. TCP has additional simultaneous-open paths, so the full state machine is richer than one ESTABLISHED-only rule.

1. A processed peer FIN leaves the local sending direction open in CLOSE_WAIT.

options.explanation: Off by one. 300 bytes starting at 1001 occupy 1001 to 1300 inclusive, so the next number, used by the FIN, is 1301.

options.text: FIN seq=1301, ACK 1301
options.explanation: The FIN's sequence number is right, but a FIN consumes a sequence number of its own, so acknowledging it means asking for 1302.

options.text: FIN seq=1301, ACK 1302
options.explanation: Correct. The data takes 1001 to 1300, the FIN takes 1301, and the server's ACK names the next number it expects: 1302.

options.text: FIN seq=1001, ACK 1002

questions.workedExample:
1. Data: 300 bytes starting at 1001.

```
first byte = 1001
last byte  = 1001 + 300 - 1 = 1300
```

2. The server ACKs the data with `ack=1301`.
3. The FIN uses the next number: **seq=1301**.
4. Like a SYN, a FIN **consumes one sequence number**, so the server acknowledges it with **ack=1302**.

This is why a peer can tell 'I have all your data' (ack=1301) apart from 'I have all your data **and** your FIN' (ack=1302).

questions.prompt: On a Linux kernel built with SYN-cookie support and tcp_syncookies = 1, an overflowing SYN backlog triggers cookie mode for a new attempt. What is the main mechanism?

options.text: It doubles the SYN queue each time it fills, until memory runs out
options.explanation: Cookie mode avoids retaining the normal per-attempt half-open entry. It still uses shared secrets, processing time and network capacity.

options.text: It drops all SYNs from IP addresses it hasn't seen before
options.explanation: That is not the cookie mechanism. Source filtering may help separately, depending on reliable information and deployment.

options.text: It requires the client to solve a proof-of-work puzzle in the SYN
options.explanation: TCP has no such mechanism, and unmodified clients must keep working. SYN cookies need no client changes at all.

options.text: It omits the normal half-open entry, encodes reconstructable state in the sequence-number construction, and validates the returning ACK before creating the connection
options.explanation: Correct. The ACK acknowledges the cookie sequence number. Validation uses secret-dependent information and freshness checks; it reduces state-exhaustion risk without eliminating CPU/bandwidth costs or every possible guess.

questions.workedExample:

2. Under overflow-triggered cookie mode, the server instead generates a checkable sequence number without keeping that ordinary entry.
3. A responding client acknowledges the sequence number, modulo 2^32.
4. The server validates the acknowledgement according to its implementation and reconstructs supported state.
5. An off-path spoofer lacking the response has to guess; a finite authenticator is not impossible to guess, and other server resources can still be exhausted.

options.explanation: That is the passive closer's path, which starts by receiving a FIN while ESTABLISHED. Both sides here sent a FIN first.

options.text: FIN_WAIT_1 → CLOSING → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED
options.explanation: Correct. Each side is in FIN_WAIT_1 when the other's FIN arrives, ACKs it and moves to CLOSING; when its own FIN is ACKed it enters TIME_WAIT. Both sides wait 2×MSL.

options.text: FIN_WAIT_1 → CLOSED, skipping TIME_WAIT because neither side was the active closer
options.explanation: In a simultaneous close both are active closers, so both must guard against stray segments; both end in TIME_WAIT.

questions.workedExample:
Follow side A (B is symmetric):

1. A calls `close()`, sends FIN: **FIN_WAIT_1**.
2. Before A's FIN is acknowledged, B's FIN arrives. A ACKs it. The state table says FIN_WAIT_1 + recv FIN goes to **CLOSING**.
3. B's ACK of A's FIN arrives: CLOSING + recv ACK goes to **TIME_WAIT**.
4. After 2×MSL: **CLOSED**.

```
FIN_WAIT_1 -FIN-> CLOSING
CLOSING    -ACK-> TIME_WAIT
TIME_WAIT  -2MSL-> CLOSED
```

Both sides end up in TIME_WAIT.

questions.prompt: An off-path attacker knows the 4-tuple of a long-lived BGP session and floods it with forged RSTs, guessing sequence numbers. One forged RST lands inside the receive window but not on the exact next expected sequence number. What does a stack that implements RFC 5961 do?

options.text: Tears the connection down, because any in-window RST is valid
options.explanation: That was the older RFC 793 behaviour, and it is exactly what made blind reset attacks practical: the attacker only had to land somewhere in a large window.

options.text: Sends a challenge ACK; only an RST with the exact expected sequence number resets the connection
options.explanation: Correct for the stated established-connection RFC 5961 rule. A rate-limited challenge ACK may be used. The mechanism improves resistance to blind resets; it is not peer authentication or proof that side channels cannot exist.

options.text: Silently ignores every RST on an established connection
options.explanation: RST must still work, or crashed and rebooted peers could never clear stale connections. RFC 5961 narrows acceptance; it doesn't remove it.

options.text: Replies with its own RST to the attacker's source address
options.explanation: The specified response is a challenge ACK toward the claimed peer, not a reset. It asks the peer’s TCP state to respond consistently; this is not a cryptographic proof.

questions.workedExample:
1. The older in-window test accepted a range of possible sequence values. In a simplified stationary 65,536-byte window, a uniform random 32-bit guess hits that range with probability 1/65,536.
2. RFC 5961’s established-state rule accepts an exact RCV.NXT match as a reset; an in-window nonmatch triggers a challenge ACK, subject to limiting; out-of-window resets are discarded.
3. In an idealised stationary state with no feedback, guessing one exact 32-bit value is harder. Real state motion, rate limits, side channels and deployment details prevent interpreting this as a measured attack cost or complete authentication.

lessons.title: Sequence numbers, ACKs and retransmission
lessons.summary: How TCP turns a lossy packet network into a reliable byte stream: cumulative ACKs, SACK, the RTO calculation from RFC 6298, fast retransmit on duplicate ACKs, and modern loss detection with RACK-TLP.
lessons.body:
IP makes no promises. Packets are dropped when a router queue overflows, corrupted by a bad link, reordered when they take different paths, and occasionally duplicated. TCP provides an ordered byte stream, suppresses duplicate delivery within a connection and retransmits detected losses. Connections can fail after partial delivery, checksums are not perfect, and an error does not tell the sender exactly what the peer application processed. This is not exactly-once application execution.

The trick is old and simple. Number every byte, have the receiver say what it has, and resend whatever seems to be missing. The hard part is deciding *when* something is missing. Resend too early and you waste bandwidth on data that was only delayed; resend too late and the connection stalls. Most of this lesson is about that judgement.

## Numbering bytes, not packets

TCP's sequence numbers count **bytes**. A segment with `seq=1001` carrying 500 bytes holds bytes 1001 to 1500. The next segment starts at 1501.

Counting bytes rather than packets lets TCP **re-segment**: if a retransmission can be bigger or smaller than the original, the receiver doesn't care, because it only tracks byte ranges.

The sequence number is 32 bits, so it wraps after 4 GiB. At an ideal TCP payload rate of 10 Gbit/s, ignoring headers and control sequence positions, that takes about 3.4 seconds, which is shorter than a segment might linger in the network. The **timestamp option** ([RFC 7323](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7323)) supports **PAWS** (Protection Against Wrapped Sequences): negotiated timestamps and serial-number comparisons against maintained timestamp state help reject old duplicates. Timestamp wrap, idle expiry, segment validation and reset handling mean this is not simply “drop anything older than the largest timestamp ever seen”.

## Cumulative acknowledgements

The receiver's ACK number means "I have **every byte before this one**". That is a **cumulative** ACK. It has two nice properties:

- A later cumulative ACK can cover data acknowledged by a lost ACK; if no later ACK arrives, loss can still delay progress.
- The receiver can ACK every other segment instead of every one (delayed ACK, lesson 4).

Its weakness shows when something in the middle is lost. Suppose the sender sends five 1,000-byte segments and the second is dropped:

```
Sender                     Receiver
seq=1    ------------->    ACK 1001
seq=1001 ----X (lost)
seq=2001 ------------->    ACK 1001
seq=3001 ------------->    ACK 1001
seq=4001 ------------->    ACK 1001
```

The receiver has bytes 2001–5000, but a cumulative ACK can only say "I'm still waiting for 1001". Those repeated ACKs are **duplicate ACKs**.

This sequence-space model merges received byte intervals, including overlap, and advances its cumulative point when gaps fill. It tracks coverage only: no payload comparison, sequence-number wrap, window limits, SYN/FIN, socket delivery, ACK timing or memory bounds. Nonnegative ordinary integer byte positions and positive interval lengths are required:

```python
def rx(arrivals, nxt=1):
    if type(nxt) is not int or nxt < 0:
        raise ValueError("bad start")
    held = []  # half-open intervals
    for seq, n in arrivals:
        if (type(seq) is not int
                or type(n) is not int
                or seq < 0 or n <= 0):
            raise ValueError("bad interval")
        merged = []
        for lo, hi in sorted(
                held + [[seq, seq + n]]):
            joins = (merged and
                     lo <= merged[-1][1])
            if joins:
                merged[-1][1] = max(
                    merged[-1][1], hi)
            else:
                merged.append([lo, hi])
        held = []
        for lo, hi in merged:
            if lo <= nxt:
                nxt = max(nxt, hi)
            else:
                held.append([lo, hi])
        print("ACK", nxt, "held",
              [lo for lo, hi in held])

rx([(1, 1000), (2001, 1000), (3001, 1000),
    (4001, 1000), (1001, 1000)])
```

Output:

```
ACK 1001 held []
ACK 1001 held [2001]
ACK 1001 held [2001]
ACK 1001 held [2001]
ACK 5001 held []
```

When the retransmitted 1001 arrives, the ACK leaps from 1001 to 5001: the receiver had the rest all along.

## Selective acknowledgement (SACK)

Cumulative ACKs leave the sender guessing. Was only 1001 lost, or 1001 and 3001? A cautious sender (**Go-Back-N** style) resends everything from 1001; an optimistic one resends 1001 and waits a round trip to learn more.

**SACK** ([RFC 2018](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2018)) lets the receiver list the blocks it holds beyond the cumulative point:

```
ACK 1001  SACK 2001-5001
```

These blocks report received ranges with exclusive right edges. They help identify gaps, but a missing report is not proof of loss: only a limited number of blocks fit, data may still be in flight, and a receiver can discard previously SACKed data before cumulative acknowledgement. Permission to send SACK is advertised directionally with `SACK-permitted` in SYN segments; support and configuration vary. A SACK option fits at most **four** blocks, or **three** alongside the timestamp option, because TCP options are limited to 40 bytes.

A related extension, **D-SACK** ([RFC 2883](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2883)), uses the first SACK block to report a segment received **twice**. Duplicate receipt can support inference of a **spurious** retransmission and possible congestion-control undo, but can also result from network duplication. The sender must apply its algorithm’s checks; D-SACK is not unconditional proof of a particular cause or automatic permission to undo every reduction.

## The retransmission timeout (RTO)

The safety net is a timer. RFC 6298’s timer starts when outstanding data needs timing, restarts on an ACK acknowledging new data, and stops when all outstanding data is acknowledged. On expiry, the earliest unacknowledged segment is retransmitted. Thus expiry is not always exactly one RTO after that segment’s original send.

The RTO must be a bit longer than a typical round trip, but RTTs vary from microseconds in a data centre to seconds on a satellite link, and they change during a connection. So TCP **measures** them. [RFC 6298](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6298) defines the calculation, which Van Jacobson introduced in 1988.

It keeps a smoothed RTT (SRTT) and a smoothed mean deviation (RTTVAR), with α = 1/8 and β = 1/4:

```
first sample R:
  SRTT   = R
  RTTVAR = R / 2

each later sample R:
  RTTVAR = (1-b)*RTTVAR + b*|SRTT - R|
  SRTT   = (1-a)*SRTT   + a*R

RTO = SRTT + max(G, 4 * RTTVAR)
```

`G` is the clock granularity. RTTVAR is updated **before** SRTT, using the old SRTT.

> [!example] Two samples
> Ignoring the minimum RTO floor and assuming clock granularity is below 4×RTTVAR:
> First sample 100 ms: SRTT = 100, RTTVAR = 50, RTO = 100 + 200 = 300 ms.
>
> Second sample 120 ms: RTTVAR = 0.75 × 50 + 0.25 × 20 = 42.5. SRTT = 0.875 × 100 + 0.125 × 120 = 102.5. RTO = 102.5 + 170 = 272.5 ms.

The `4 × RTTVAR` term is the important one. A connection with a steady RTT gets a tight timeout; a jittery one gets a generous margin, so it doesn't fire on every delay spike.

Other rules:

- **Minimum RTO.** RFC 6298 says a computed value below one second SHOULD be rounded up to one second. The retrieved Linux documentation lists a **200 ms default**, with route, socket and sysctl overrides; it is not a hard universal lower bound.
- **Initial RTO** before measurement: RFC 6298 recommends one second and permits a more conservative value.
- **Exponential backoff.** Each time the timer fires for the same data, the RTO doubles (an optional RFC 6298 maximum must be at least 60 s; the retrieved Linux default maximum is 120 s and is configurable). This stops a sender hammering a path that is down.
- **Karn's algorithm.** Without a mechanism that disambiguates the measurement, do not take an RTT sample from retransmitted data: when the ACK arrives you can't tell whether it acknowledges the original or the copy. Negotiated timestamp echo rules can remove this ambiguity and permit such samples; the echo is selected by those rules, not invariably from the latest segment that triggered an ACK.

A timeout delays recovery. Under RFC 5681, the loss window after an RTO is at most one full-sized segment; this is a congestion-window change, not a specified one-segment-per-second rate. Linux documents `tcp_retries2 = 15` using a hypothetical default timeout of 924.6 seconds as a lower bound under its stated backoff model. Actual failure time depends on timers, overrides and application policy. An entirely idle connection with no outstanding data need not discover a vanished peer without probes or keepalives.

## Fast retransmit

Waiting for a timeout is slow. The duplicate ACKs from earlier are a quicker signal: repeated cumulative ACKs can indicate out-of-order arrival, although duplicate packets/ACKs and other events complicate that inference. Classic algorithms apply a specific duplicate-ACK definition, including window/data conditions.

One duplicate could just be **reordering**: two packets swapped places. So the classic rule ([RFC 5681](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5681)) waits for **three duplicate ACKs**, then retransmits the missing segment straight away, without waiting for the timer. That is **fast retransmit**, usually paired with **fast recovery** (lesson 5) to control the congestion window during recovery. Reno’s multiplicative reduction does not promise the application’s measured sending rate is exactly halved.

```
ACK 1001          (new data acked)
ACK 1001  dup #1
ACK 1001  dup #2
ACK 1001  dup #3  -> resend seq=1001
ACK 5001          (hole filled)
```

Fast retransmit needs **enough data after the loss** to generate three duplicates. Without additional mechanisms such as Limited Transmit or loss probes, the simple three-duplicate threshold can fail to trigger in these cases:

- **Small windows**: if only three segments are in flight and one is lost, at most two duplicates come back.
- **Tail loss**: if the **last** segment of a response is lost, nothing follows it, so no duplicates arrive at all. The simple scheme may then need the RTO; other loss-recovery mechanisms can intervene.

## Modern loss detection: RACK-TLP

Counting duplicate ACKs is crude. **RACK-TLP** ([RFC 8985](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8985)), reasons about transmission and acknowledgement **time**. The retrieved Linux documentation describes RACK support; availability and defaults in other systems require version-specific confirmation.

- **RACK** (Recent ACKnowledgement) uses delivery of later-transmitted data, transmission times, an RTT estimate and a reordering window to infer losses of earlier unacknowledged transmissions. ACK/SACK information can provide this evidence; duplicate-ACK count alone is not the trigger. Reordering tolerance can adapt using D-SACK and other state.
- **TLP** (Tail Loss Probe) schedules a probe timeout whose baseline is 2×SRTT. Rules account for unavailable RTT estimates, possible delayed ACKs, the RTO deadline and probe eligibility. It prefers new data when available and permitted; otherwise it can retransmit the highest-sequence segment. A probe/ACK exchange may expose earlier tail loss to RACK. It does not guarantee delivery or a fixed total repair time.

| Mechanism | Main trigger | Timing qualification |
|---|---|---|
| RTO | Retransmission timer expires | Estimator, floor/cap and backoff apply |
| Classic fast retransmit | 3 qualifying duplicate ACKs | Depends on ACK arrivals |
| RACK | Delivery/time evidence of a hole | RTT and reordering state apply |
| TLP | Eligible probe timeout expires | Baseline 2×SRTT, with adjustments |

## Pitfalls and real-world notes

- **Reordering looks like loss.** Multipath links and some load balancers reorder packets, which can trigger spurious fast retransmits and needless slowdowns. RACK's adaptive window and D-SACK undo help, and per-flow ECMP hashing can reduce reordering caused by per-packet path changes.
- **Checksums are weak.** TCP's 16-bit checksum misses some multi-bit errors. Real systems lean on link-layer CRCs and, increasingly, TLS, whose authenticated records detect alteration with a very small but nonzero forgery probability under their cryptographic assumptions. Neither layer gives a mathematical guarantee against every error.
- **Transport acknowledgement is not application acknowledgement.** A cumulative ACK means the peer’s **TCP endpoint** accepted the preceding stream positions, not that the application processed them. If you need "the server saved it", you need an application-level acknowledgement.
- **Retransmission rate is a health signal.** On Linux, `ss -ti` shows per-connection `rto`, `rtt` and `retrans`, and `nstat` shows `TcpRetransSegs`. Interpret retransmission counters with their definitions, denominator, traffic pattern and captures; no universal one-percent threshold identifies a cause.

## Key takeaways
- TCP numbers bytes; the 32-bit space wraps quickly at high speed, so timestamps (PAWS) disambiguate old segments.
- A cumulative ACK says "I have everything before N". Out-of-order arrivals produce duplicate ACKs.
- SACK reports selected received ranges (option space limits the count); D-SACK reports duplicate receipt, which can support recovery diagnostics.
- The RTO estimator is SRTT + max(G, 4×RTTVAR), subject to timer policy, bounds and backoff; Karn’s rule avoids ambiguous RTT samples.
- Classic fast retransmit uses three qualifying duplicate ACKs; without additional mechanisms, insufficient following data can leave tail losses or small flights waiting for the timer.
- RACK-TLP detects loss by time and probes the tail, turning many timeouts into quick repairs.

questions.prompt: A TCP segment has `seq=5001` and carries 1,200 bytes of data. What is the number of its last byte, and what sequence number will the next segment start at? Assume ordinary contiguous new data, no SYN/FIN and that the receiver already has all earlier data in this connection.

options.text: Last byte 6201, next segment 6202
options.explanation: This counts one byte too many. Bytes 5001 up to and including 6200 are exactly 1,200 bytes.

options.text: Last byte 6200, next segment 6201
options.explanation: Correct. The segment covers 5001 to 5001 + 1200 − 1 = 6200, so the next byte is 6201.

options.text: Last byte 5002, next segment 5003
options.explanation: This treats sequence numbers as counting segments. TCP numbers bytes, so a 1,200-byte segment advances the number by 1,200.

options.text: It depends on the MSS of the next segment
options.explanation: Under the stated contiguous-new-data assumption, the next byte is 6201 regardless of the next segment’s length. Retransmissions could begin at other earlier sequence positions.

questions.workedExample:
1. TCP sequence numbers count **bytes**.
2. First byte = 5001. With 1,200 bytes:

```
last = 5001 + 1200 - 1 = 6200
next = 6200 + 1        = 6201
```

3. The receiver will ACK this segment with `ack=6201` (the next byte it wants).

questions.prompt: A receiver sends `ACK 3001` without any SACK option. What exactly does that tell the sender? Interpret this as a current cumulative ACK within one unwrapped sequence interval, not an old duplicate ACK or a SYN/FIN boundary.

options.text: The receiver got the segment whose sequence number is 3001
options.explanation: The ACK number is the next byte wanted, not the last one received. Byte 3001 has not arrived yet.

options.text: The receiver has bytes up to 3001 but may be missing some earlier ones
options.explanation: A cumulative ACK can't have gaps below it. It promises everything before the number.

options.text: The receiver has received exactly 3,001 bytes in total since the handshake
options.explanation: Sequence numbers start at a random ISN, not at zero, so the ACK number doesn't count bytes received.

options.text: The receiver has every byte before 3001, and 3001 is the next byte it expects
options.explanation: Correct. TCP ACKs are cumulative. It may also hold later out-of-order bytes, but without SACK it can't say so.

questions.workedExample: In the stated sequence interval, ACK 3001 identifies the next expected position. Preceding data in this connection has been accepted contiguously by TCP; later ranges may also be buffered. This says neither how many total bytes have ever arrived nor whether the application consumed or stored them. Sequence wrap and old ACKs require the connection’s serial-number context.

questions.prompt: Classic fast retransmit waits for **three** duplicate ACKs before resending. Why not resend as soon as the first duplicate arrives?

options.text: A single duplicate ACK can result from packet reordering rather than loss
options.explanation: Correct. Waiting for more evidence reduces sensitivity to modest reordering. Three duplicates can still occur without actual loss, so it is a heuristic rather than proof.

options.text: Because the receiver only sends duplicate ACKs in threes
options.explanation: The threshold is a sender-side algorithm rule. Receivers often promptly ACK out-of-order data, but ACK loss, duplication and coalescing can change the observed pattern.

options.text: To give the retransmission timer a chance to fire first
options.explanation: Fast retransmit is intended to recover before RTO expiry when enough qualifying duplicate ACKs arrive; there is no universal ordering between an arbitrary few RTTs and the configured timer.

options.text: Because the receiver's window must open by three segments
options.explanation: The threshold is used for loss inference, not a requirement to increase the window by three segments. The classic duplicate-ACK definition does include an unchanged advertised-window condition.

questions.workedExample:
1. Suppose segments A, B, C are sent and B is delayed slightly so the order becomes A, C, B.
2. After C the receiver sends a duplicate ACK (still waiting for B). When B arrives, the ACK jumps past C.
3. If the sender had resent B on the first duplicate, that retransmission would be wasted, and a congestion response could reduce its sending allowance unnecessarily.
4. In the simple example with one ACK per arrival, three duplicates provide stronger evidence of a hole; they do not universally prove three distinct later segments or actual loss. Modern RACK uses timing instead of a count for the same reason.

questions.prompt:
Using the lesson's toy receiver, what does this print?

```python
rx([(1, 500), (1001, 500),
    (501, 500), (1501, 500)])
```

options.text: ACKs 501, 1501, 1501, 2001; nothing ever held
options.explanation: This assumes the segment at 1001 is accepted in order. It arrives while the receiver is still waiting for 501, so it is held, and the ACK stays at 501.

options.text: ACKs 501, 501, 1001, 2001; 1001 still held after the third line
options.explanation: When 501–1000 fills the gap, it joins the held 1001–1500 interval and the cumulative point advances to 1501. That held range no longer remains outstanding.

options.text: ACKs 501, 501, 1501, 2001; 1001 held only on the second line
options.explanation: Correct. The model merges adjacent received ranges and advances across their combined coverage once the gap fills.

options.text: ACKs 501, 1501, 1501, 2001; 1001 held on the second line
options.explanation: A cumulative ACK can't move past a hole. With 501–1000 missing, the ACK must stay at 501.

questions.workedExample:
Start with nxt = 1 and no held intervals.

1. (1, 500) covers [1,501), so print `ACK 501 held []`.
2. (1001, 500) covers [1001,1501), beyond the gap; print `ACK 501 held [1001]`.
3. (501, 500) joins it into [501,1501), so print `ACK 1501 held []`.
4. (1501, 500) extends coverage to 2001; print `ACK 2001 held []`.

The printed held list contains starts of merged ranges, not one entry per original packet.

questions.prompt: A connection currently has SRTT = 100 ms and RTTVAR = 50 ms. A new RTT sample of 120 ms arrives. Using RFC 6298 (α = 1/8, β = 1/4, ignoring clock granularity and minimums), what is the new RTO?

options.text: 120 ms
options.explanation: The RTO is not the latest sample. It is a smoothed estimate plus a safety margin of four deviations.

options.text: 300 ms
options.explanation: That is the RTO before this sample (100 + 4 × 50). The new sample changes both SRTT and RTTVAR.

options.text: 205 ms
options.explanation: Even 102.5 + 2 × 42.5 would be 187.5 ms, not 205 ms. The specified estimator uses four times RTTVAR, producing 272.5 ms before bounds.

questions.workedExample:
Update RTTVAR first, using the **old** SRTT:

```
|SRTT - R| = |100 - 120| = 20
RTTVAR = 0.75*50 + 0.25*20
       = 37.5 + 5 = 42.5
```

Then SRTT:

```
SRTT = 0.875*100 + 0.125*120
     = 87.5 + 15 = 102.5
```

Then the timeout:

```
RTO = 102.5 + 4*42.5
    = 102.5 + 170 = 272.5 ms
```

A configured 200 ms floor would not change this estimate; the RFC’s recommended one-second floor would. The question explicitly omits those bounds, and this arithmetic does not reproduce every implementation’s estimator.

questions.prompt: In a simplified classic Reno model using the three-duplicate-ACK trigger, no Limited Transmit/TLP/RACK, no new data beyond the stated flight and one qualifying duplicate ACK per out-of-order arrival, which losses may require the RTO? Assume ACKs themselves are delivered. Select all that apply.

options.text: An API returns a 3-segment response and the last segment is lost
options.explanation: Correct. Nothing is sent after the lost segment, so the receiver has no reason to send any duplicate ACKs. This tail loss waits for the timer (or for TLP).

options.text: A bulk transfer has 40 segments in flight and the 10th is lost
options.explanation: Thirty segments arrive after the hole, each producing a duplicate ACK, so three duplicates arrive quickly and fast retransmit works.

options.text: Only 3 segments are in flight and the first is lost
options.explanation: Correct. Only two later segments arrive, so only two duplicate ACKs come back, one short of the threshold.

options.text: The fast retransmission is itself lost, with no additional recovery mechanism or new acknowledgement progress
options.explanation: Correct under the specified simplified recovery model. Repeated ACKs for the same gap do not establish a new recovery event; the RTO remains the fallback. Other algorithms can recover differently.

options.text: Two adjacent segments exchange arrival order and none is lost
options.explanation: There's no loss to repair here. At most one duplicate ACK is sent, so fast retransmit correctly doesn't fire.

questions.workedExample: Under these assumptions: tail loss has no following data to generate duplicate ACKs; the three-segment flight with its first segment lost has only two later arrivals; a lost retransmission has no additional recovery mechanism. Those cases can need the timer. The bulk flight provides enough delivered later data for the threshold. Adjacent reordering without loss has no loss to repair. Real stacks may use additional mechanisms.
