options.text: About 50 ms
options.explanation: This treats 500 KB as 500 kilobits. Convert bytes to bits first: 500 KB is 4 Mbit.

options.text: About 4 ms
options.explanation: This is off by a factor of 100. 4 Mbit at 10 Mbit/s takes 0.4 s to drain.

options.text: About 0.4 s
None, because CUBIC avoids filling buffers
options.explanation: The question supplies a backlog. Neither CUBIC nor BBR guarantees that queues remain empty.

questions.workedExample: 500,000 bytes × 8 / 10,000,000 bit/s = 0.4 seconds. This is the waiting time behind the specified backlog. CoDel’s 5 ms default target is not a hard guarantee for every packet.

questions.prompt: Which of these are genuine features of QUIC compared with TCP plus TLS? Select all that apply.

options.text: It combines transport and TLS setup and can support eligible 0-RTT early data
options.explanation: Correct. Prior state/configuration is required for early data; rejection, replay concerns, Retry or loss can alter timing.

options.text: Its per-stream ordering avoids making one stream wait solely for missing bytes on another stream
options.explanation: Correct. Shared congestion control, flow control and application dependencies can still affect several streams.

options.text: Connection IDs can support client address changes when migration conditions are satisfied
options.explanation: Correct. Negotiated restrictions, handshake state, usable connection IDs, path validation and reachability matter; seamless success is not guaranteed.

options.text: It delivers all streams' data in one global order, like TCP
options.explanation: That would reintroduce head-of-line blocking. Ordering is per stream only.

options.text: It is implemented in the OS kernel, which makes it faster to deploy
options.explanation: QUIC can run in user-space libraries or other implementation locations. Its specification does not require a kernel implementation.

questions.workedExample: The first three describe protocol capabilities with their conditions. QUIC does not impose a single global stream delivery order, and its specification does not dictate kernel placement.

questions.prompt: A previously idle CoDel queue uses target 5 ms and interval 100 ms. No hard buffer limit is reached. Case A spikes to 40 ms but empties within 20 ms. Case B remains at 30–40 ms for seconds with sufficient backlog to satisfy CoDel’s remaining-byte check. Which behaviour is expected?

options.text: It drops packets in both cases, because delay exceeded 5 ms
options.explanation: Exceeding the target briefly does not alone trigger CoDel’s persistent-delay response. A burst could still encounter a finite-buffer limit, which this question excludes.

options.text: It drops in case A only, because sudden spikes are the problem
options.explanation: Bursts are what buffers exist for. The harmful case is the standing queue in B, which adds delay without adding throughput.

options.text: It doesn't drop in either case; CoDel only drops when the buffer is full
options.explanation: CoDel can signal persistent queueing before the buffer fills. It also retains checks intended to avoid starving the link.

options.text: It leaves case A alone, and in case B starts dropping (or ECN-marking), at increasing frequency while the delay stays above target
options.explanation: Correct. In B, the minimum delay over every 100 ms interval stays above 5 ms, which signals a standing queue. Responsive senders can reduce their offered load; the response depends on the protocol, controller and delivered feedback.

questions.workedExample: Case A clears before a full interval of excessive delay, so it does not trigger the persistent-delay response under these assumptions. Case B satisfies both the persistent-delay and backlog conditions and enters dropping/marking behaviour. The control law schedules increasingly frequent signals using interval divided by the square root of the count. Actual delay still depends on traffic response; 5 ms is a target, not a per-packet guarantee.

questions.prompt: Within a QUIC packet-number space, each newly sent packet gets a new increasing packet number, even when it resends stream data. Which TCP retransmission ambiguity does this remove?

options.text: Packets are smaller, because packet numbers are shorter than sequence numbers
options.explanation: Size isn't the point; QUIC packet numbers can be encoded compactly, but the real gain is unambiguous acknowledgements.

options.text: An ACK identifies which numbered packet transmission arrived, removing original-versus-retransmission ambiguity for that packet
options.explanation: Correct. Other estimation errors and spurious loss declarations remain possible; packet numbers do not make all loss detection infallible.

options.text: Data never needs to be retransmitted
options.explanation: Lost data must still be resent; it is simply sent in a new packet with a new number, with stream offsets keeping the data's position.

options.text: It allows middleboxes to reorder packets correctly
options.explanation: Packet numbers have header protection. An observer can derive Initial protection keys, so “middleboxes can never read any packet numbers” would also be too strong.

questions.workedExample: TCP reuses byte sequence numbers when resending data, so an ACK may not reveal which copy caused it; Karn’s rule or timestamps address RTT-sampling ambiguity. QUIC identifies packet transmissions separately from stream offsets, within each packet-number space. This removes that particular ambiguity. ACK delay, sampling choices and reordering still require careful recovery logic.

questions.prompt: Which mechanisms can make transport extensions harder to deploy or help QUIC evolve? Select all that apply.

options.text: Some middleboxes interfere with unfamiliar TCP options or SYN data
options.explanation: Correct. Compatibility and fallback matter; this is not a claim that every middlebox behaves this way.

options.text: A TCP change in a kernel stack can depend on OS deployment cycles; a QUIC library can be updated with an application
options.explanation: Correct. Some TCP changes are sender-only, and neither TCP nor QUIC is required to live exclusively in one implementation layer.

options.text: Protecting QUIC control frames and selected header fields reduces the information middleboxes can depend on
options.explanation: Correct. Some wire fields remain visible and Initial keys are publicly derivable, so encryption does not eliminate all ossification or interference.

options.text: The TCP header has no room for any options
options.explanation: The base TCP header allows up to 40 option bytes. That finite space can constrain extensions too, but it is not zero; unfamiliar-option handling by middleboxes is a separate deployment obstacle.

options.text: The IETF has forbidden new TCP extensions since QUIC was standardised
options.explanation: TCP is still being extended (for example RACK-TLP in 2021 and AccECN work). Deployment, not permission, is the barrier.

questions.workedExample: The first three describe compatibility, implementation deployment and protection mechanisms. The base TCP header permits up to 40 option bytes, and TCP standards work continues. None of these mechanisms guarantees a fixed adoption speed.

questions.prompt: A phone loses its old Wi-Fi path and gains a new address on 5G. Compare ordinary TCP (without MPTCP or an address-preserving tunnel) with a confirmed QUIC connection using usable connection IDs. Assume active migration is allowed and the new path passes validation and remains reachable. Which connection can continue at the transport level?

options.text: Both continue seamlessly, because the server recognises the device
options.explanation: TCP has no concept of a device; a connection is its 4-tuple. A new client IP is a different connection as far as TCP is concerned.

options.text: Both break; the application must resume the download in either case
options.explanation: Under the supplied conditions, QUIC can migrate the existing connection to the new path.

options.text: Ordinary TCP cannot move the existing connection to the new address; QUIC can continue through migration
options.explanation: Correct under the stated assumptions. QUIC still needs appropriate path validation and congestion-control handling; this does not promise no interruption.

An application can reconnect and resume if its protocol supports that. QUIC connection IDs allow the established connection to be found from a new address; validation and path-state changes still apply. The question explicitly supplies successful migration conditions rather than assuming every network change succeeds.

lessons.title: The sockets API and a Python server
lessons.summary: How Berkeley socket calls map onto TCP's states and queues, why TCP has no message boundaries and how to frame messages, partial sends and EOF, SO_REUSEADDR, and building a correct Python server with threads and with an event loop.
lessons.body:
Python's **socket API** wraps operating-system networking interfaces. Similar concepts appear in other languages, but high-level runtimes, platforms and socket modes differ in their errors, buffering and lifetime rules.

This lesson separates byte-stream framing from connection setup and demonstrates bounded-message helpers. The servers remain teaching examples; the selector example is deliberately faulty for a debugging exercise.

## The calls and what they do in TCP

```
Server                 Client
socket()               socket()
bind(port)
listen(backlog)        connect(addr)
   SYN queue  <-- SYN ----
              --- SYN+ACK -->
   accept q   <-- ACK ----  (returns)
accept()  (returns a new socket)
recv()/send()  <------>  send()/recv()
close()        <-FIN/ACK->  close()
```

| Call | What happens in the kernel |
|---|---|
| `socket()` | Creates an endpoint; state CLOSED |
| `bind()` | Associates a local address/port, subject to reuse rules |
| `listen(n)` | State LISTEN; creates the queues |
| `connect()` | Ordinary blocking TCP: initiates setup, then succeeds or fails; non-blocking mode differs |
| `accept()` | Returns a new connected socket from pending connections |
| `close()` | Releases this socket reference; final closure can initiate FIN or an abort, depending on state/options |

Two points surprise people:

- **`accept()` does not perform the handshake.** The kernel completes handshakes on its own, whether or not the application is calling `accept()`. In ordinary TCP it dequeues a completed connection and returns a **new** socket; the peer may already have sent FIN before acceptance. Fast Open can allow acceptance before the normal handshake finishes. The listener remains available.
- **Ordinary blocking `connect()` success means the client-side handshake progressed successfully**, not that the server application accepted you or processed data. Queue overflow can leave the server still waiting to complete its side.

## The backlog and the two queues

A useful Linux model distinguishes two kinds of pending state (SYN cookies can avoid allocating an entry per SYN):

1. The **SYN queue**: half-open connections waiting for the final ACK.
2. The **accept queue**: completed connections waiting for `accept()`.

The `backlog` argument to `listen()` sets the size of the **accept queue**, capped by `net.core.somaxconn` (4,096 by default since Linux 5.4; 128 before).

If the application is too slow to accept and that queue fills, one Linux path with `tcp_abort_on_overflow = 0` can **ignore** the client's final ACK; other overload paths can drop SYNs. The client thinks it's connected and may send its request; the server retransmits SYN+ACK and the connection completes later, or not. The symptom is clients seeing occasional multi-second delays on connect or first request. `nstat` shows `TcpExtListenOverflows` climbing.

> [!tip] Investigate queue overload
> Arrival bursts, slow acceptance, resource limits and backlog configuration can all contribute. Inspect application scheduling and queue/counter measurements. A growing overflow counter does not by itself identify a single cause or prove one packet-level sequence.

## A stream has no message boundaries

TCP delivers a **byte stream**. It does not preserve the boundaries of your `send()` calls:

```
client: send(b"hello")
client: send(b"world")

server recv(1024) may return:
  b"helloworld"         (coalesced)
  b"hel", then b"loworld" (split)
  b"hello", then b"world"
```

All three are correct TCP behaviour. Nagle, segmentation, retransmission and the timing of `recv()` calls all affect where the cuts fall. A one-read-per-message assumption can fail even on localhost; a passing local test does not establish framing correctness.

Protocols that distinguish messages need **framing**. A single stream-to-EOF transfer can use EOF as its boundary:

- **Length prefix**: send a fixed-size length, then that many bytes. For example, gRPC has its own message-length prefix inside HTTP/2 DATA frames; the HTTP/2 frame header is a separate framing layer.
- **Delimiter**: end each message with a marker, such as `\r\n` in SMTP and in HTTP/1.1 headers. The receiver buffers until it finds one.
- **Protocol-defined body rules**: HTTP/1.1 uses status/method rules, `Content-Length`, chunked encoding, or connection closure as applicable; not every response has a body.

## Partial reads, partial writes and EOF

Three rules for using the calls correctly:

1. For a positive `n`, ordinary blocking **`recv(n)` returns at most n bytes**. Short reads are allowed. Flags, low-water settings, timeouts and errors can change when it returns; loop for a specified length.
2. **`send()` may send only part of the buffer**, returning the count it accepted, for example because of limited buffer capacity. Python's `sendall()` handles partial writes on blocking sockets, but may raise; success means local acceptance, not peer processing.
3. With a positive read size and no local receive shutdown, **`recv()` returning `b""` indicates end of stream** after received bytes have been consumed: the peer closed its sending direction. It is not an error and not "no data yet". If you don't treat it as the end, you'll spin forever on a closed connection.

Error conditions show up as exceptions:

| Python exception | Usual meaning |
|---|---|
| `ConnectionRefusedError` | RST in reply to SYN |
| `ConnectionResetError` | Peer sent RST mid-connection |
| `BrokenPipeError` | Writing to a stream no longer usable for sending; peer half-close alone need not cause it |
| `TimeoutError` / `socket.timeout` | An operation exceeded its applicable timeout; `sendall()` has an overall timeout |

Choose operation timeouts and application deadlines. A silent peer can otherwise leave a blocking read waiting indefinitely. Linux’s documented default keepalive idle interval is 7,200 seconds when keepalive is enabled, but applications and configuration can change it. Keepalive is not a substitute for a request deadline.

## A length-prefixed server with threads

First, framing helpers. `recv_exact` loops until it has exactly `n` bytes, and treats EOF in the middle as an error:

```python
import socket, struct, threading

MAX_MSG = 1024 * 1024  # teaching limit

def recv_exact(sock, n):
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("invalid length")
    buf = bytearray()
    while len(buf) < n:
        chunk = sock.recv(n - len(buf))
        if not chunk:
            raise EOFError
        buf += chunk
    return bytes(buf)

def recv_msg(sock):
    hdr = recv_exact(sock, 4)
    (n,) = struct.unpack("!I", hdr)
    if n > MAX_MSG:
        raise ValueError("too large")
    return recv_exact(sock, n)

def send_msg(sock, data):
    if len(data) > MAX_MSG:
        raise ValueError("too large")
    hdr = struct.pack("!I", len(data))
    sock.sendall(hdr + data)
```

`"!I"` is a 4-byte unsigned integer in network byte order (big-endian). Combining header and body avoids an application-created pause between two small writes, but one `sendall()` is not one packet and cannot guarantee freedom from Nagle, queueing or other delays.

Then the server, one thread per connection:

```python
def handle(conn, addr):
    with conn:
        conn.settimeout(5)
        try:
            while True:
                msg = recv_msg(conn)
                send_msg(conn, msg.upper())
        except (EOFError, OSError,
                ValueError):
            pass  # toy policy: close

srv = socket.create_server(
    ("127.0.0.1", 9000), backlog=128)
while True:
    conn, addr = srv.accept()
    threading.Thread(target=handle,
                     args=(conn, addr),
                     daemon=True).start()
```

And a client:

```python
with socket.create_connection(
        ("127.0.0.1", 9000),
        timeout=5) as s:
    s.settimeout(5)
    send_msg(s, b"hello")
    print(recv_msg(s))   # b'HELLO'
```

Details that make this correct:

- `with conn:` closes this socket when the handler exits. It cannot force a handler that never exits to finish; duplicated references and wrappers also affect lifetime.
- The helpers cap each body at 1 MiB. The handler has a per-operation timeout, not a total-message deadline: a trickling peer can keep a message in progress. Production code needs total deadlines, connection/thread limits and a deliberate error policy.
- `socket.create_server` sets **`SO_REUSEADDR`** on POSIX systems. Without suitable reuse settings, retained connection state can prevent immediate rebinding. This is not an inevitable outcome of every restart; address, platform and old/new socket options matter.

> [!note] SO_REUSEADDR vs SO_REUSEPORT
> `SO_REUSEADDR` relaxes platform-specific bind rules; it does not grant arbitrary sharing with an active listener. Linux generally requires the reuse option on both the previous and new sockets for the relevant reuse case. `SO_REUSEPORT` (Linux 3.9+) supports multiple eligible listeners at the same address/port, each with its own queue. Sockets must set it before binding; Linux requires matching effective user IDs. Default selection and optional BPF policies do not guarantee perfectly balanced work.

## Scaling: threads versus an event loop

A thread per connection is simple, but stack reservations, task limits and scheduling costs constrain scale. Exact limits and stack sizes depend on the runtime and platform. Many mostly idle connections motivate multiplexing rather than one native thread each.

The alternative is **non-blocking sockets** and a **readiness API**: `select`/`poll`, `epoll` (Linux) or `kqueue` (BSD, macOS). Availability differs by platform: Python exposes `poll` on Unix, while Windows `select` handles sockets only. In the usual scanning-cost model, `select` scales with the highest descriptor number and `poll` with the number of supplied descriptors. One thread asks the kernel "which of these sockets can I read or write without blocking?" and handles only those. Python's `selectors` module chooses an available backend according to its platform policy. Readiness can become stale: non-blocking operations must still handle `BlockingIOError`.

**Deliberately faulty debugging example:** the next loop ignores partial writes and can exit on an unhandled would-block error. It is the subject of quiz question 10, not a correct echo-server template:

```python
import selectors, socket

EV = selectors.EVENT_READ
sel = selectors.DefaultSelector()
srv = socket.create_server(
    ("127.0.0.1", 9001))
srv.setblocking(False)
sel.register(srv, EV)

while True:
    for key, _ in sel.select():
        s = key.fileobj
        if s is srv:
            conn, _ = srv.accept()
            conn.setblocking(False)
            sel.register(conn, EV)
            continue
        try:
            data = s.recv(4096)
        except ConnectionError:
            data = b""
        if data:
            s.send(data)  # may be partial
        else:
            sel.unregister(s)
            s.close()
```

This loop can lose echo bytes or terminate. Correct readiness handling requires partial-write accounting, would-block/error handling for accept/read/write, bounded per-connection output queues, read backpressure, cleanup and half-close handling. Enable write interest only while output is pending and flush pending output before closing after input EOF. Frameworks provide parts of this machinery, but applications must still choose limits, framing and deadlines.

`asyncio` gives the same event-loop efficiency with sequential-looking code:

```python
import asyncio

async def handle(reader, writer):
    try:
        while True:
            data = await reader.read(4096)
            if not data:
                break
            writer.write(data.upper())
            await writer.drain()
    except ConnectionError:
        pass
    finally:
        writer.close()
        try:
            await writer.wait_closed()
        except ConnectionError:
            pass

async def main():
    srv = await asyncio.start_server(
        handle, "127.0.0.1", 9002)
    async with srv:
        await srv.serve_forever()

asyncio.run(main())
```

`writer.drain()` cooperates with the transport’s high/low watermarks: after writing is paused at the high watermark, it waits for the buffer to drain to the low watermark. It does not wait for a peer application acknowledgment. Slow readers, congestion or limited path capacity can cause backpressure; a zero receive window is not required. This echo sample has cleanup but still needs application deadlines and connection/resource limits for deployment.

## Key takeaways
- Ordinary TCP setup can progress without the application calling `accept()`; acceptance returns a separate socket.
- Linux backlog and queue overload require version/configuration-aware diagnosis.
- TCP delivers ordered bytes, not application messages. Handle short reads, partial writes and half-close explicitly.
- Bound messages and resource use, close owned sockets, and distinguish per-operation timeouts from total deadlines.
- Readiness loops must retain unsent output and apply backpressure; `asyncio.drain()` is a buffer-flow-control mechanism.

> [!note] Evidence limits
> Fixed thread-capacity and memory figures, universal restart behaviour and guaranteed load balancing are omitted: they require platform-specific measurements. The selector loop is retained only as an explicitly faulty exercise. Loopback example checks do not establish production scale, WAN behaviour or resistance to resource exhaustion.

questions.prompt: On a blocking TCP socket with no local receive shutdown, recv(4096) returns b"" after all preceding data has been consumed. What does this indicate?

options.text: No data has arrived yet; call recv() again shortly
options.explanation: A blocking recv() waits until data arrives; it never returns empty just because nothing is there yet. (A non-blocking socket raises BlockingIOError instead.)

options.text: The peer has closed its sending side (sent FIN); there will be no more data
options.explanation: Correct. An empty read is end-of-stream. Your code should stop reading and, usually, close the socket.

options.text: The peer sent an RST
options.explanation: An RST surfaces as an exception, ConnectionResetError, not as an empty read.

options.text: The receive buffer is full
options.explanation: A full buffer means there's plenty to read; recv() would return data immediately.

questions.workedExample: For this positive-length read, an empty result indicates end of the peer’s sending stream. Stop waiting for further input. A half-closed connection may still be usable for sending a response; then close or shut down according to the protocol. Forgetting EOF handling can create a busy loop, but the exact TCP state also depends on local shutdown history.

questions.prompt: An ordinary Linux TCP listener has room in its pending queues, the path is working, and no Fast Open is in use. Its process pauses in a debugger after listen(128), before accept(). Can a client’s blocking connect() succeed?

options.text: connect() succeeds: the kernel completes the handshake and queues the connection for accept()
options.explanation: Correct. Handshakes are handled by the kernel. The connection sits in the accept queue, and the client can even send data, which waits in the server's receive buffer.

options.text: connect() blocks until the server calls accept()
options.explanation: The kernel can perform the ordinary TCP handshake without the application accepting. The peer may even half-close before the server eventually accepts.

options.text: connect() fails with ConnectionRefusedError
options.explanation: Refusal (RST) happens when nothing is listening. A socket in LISTEN accepts handshakes even when its process is stuck.

options.text: connect() times out after about two minutes
options.explanation: The supplied conditions do not require waiting for acceptance or a timeout. Timeout durations are configuration-dependent.

questions.workedExample: The kernel listener can process SYN and ACK traffic while the application is paused. The client can complete its local handshake and queue data before the server calls accept(). The requested backlog is subject to platform limits and does not establish an exact universal 128-connection failure threshold.

questions.prompt: Why does a TCP application that needs to distinguish messages need a framing rule, such as a length prefix, delimiter or a defined EOF boundary?

options.text: Because TCP may reorder bytes, and framing puts them back in order
options.explanation: TCP already guarantees in-order delivery. Framing is about where messages begin and end, not order.

options.text: Because TCP limits each send() to one MSS
options.explanation: send() is not restricted to one MSS; it can accept more, or only part of the supplied buffer. Segmentation is separate from application framing.

options.text: Because TCP is a byte stream and doesn't preserve the boundaries of send() calls
options.explanation: Correct. The receiver may get two messages in one recv() or half a message, so it needs a rule for finding message boundaries.

options.text: Because framing is needed to compute TCP's checksum
options.explanation: TCP checksums cover segments, independently of application message framing. They may be computed by the protocol stack or hardware offload; a kernel implementation is not required.

questions.workedExample: TCP preserves byte order but not write boundaries. A receiver may obtain part of a message or several messages in one read. A protocol must define how to recognise its boundaries, which may include EOF. Ordinary UDP preserves the boundary of each delivered datagram, but datagrams can be lost, duplicated or truncated by an undersized receive buffer.

questions.prompt: On a fresh TCP stream with no other reader, a client successfully sends b"hello" then b"world". No local receive shutdown or connection failure occurs. Which results could the server’s first recv(1024) return? Select all that apply.

options.text: `b"helloworld"`
options.explanation: Possible. Both writes may arrive (or be coalesced into one segment) before the server reads.

options.text: `b"hel"`
options.explanation: Possible. recv() returns whatever has arrived so far, which may be a fragment of the first write.

options.text: `b"hello"`
options.explanation: Possible, and common in testing, which is why the bug of assuming it is easy to miss.

options.text: `b"world"`
options.explanation: Impossible. TCP delivers bytes in order, so the first bytes returned must start with "h".

options.text: `b"worldhello"`
options.explanation: Impossible. Reordering is never visible through a TCP socket.

questions.workedExample:
TCP delivers received stream bytes in order; it does not preserve write boundaries or promise that a connection can never fail.

1. The byte stream is `helloworld`.
2. The first `recv()` returns some non-empty **prefix** of the bytes that have arrived: `h`, `hel`, `hello`, `hellowor`, `helloworld`...
3. Anything that doesn't start at the first byte (`world`, `worldhello`) is impossible.

So A, B and C are possible.

questions.prompt:
This code works in local tests but occasionally raises `struct.error: unpack requires a buffer of 4 bytes` in production. Why?

```python
hdr = sock.recv(4)
(n,) = struct.unpack("!I", hdr)
body = sock.recv(n)
```

options.text: Network byte order is little-endian, so `!I` is wrong
options.explanation: Network byte order is big-endian, which is exactly what `!` means. The format is fine.

options.text: recv(4) can return fewer than 4 bytes, for example when the header is split across segments
options.explanation: Correct. recv(n) returns up to n bytes, whatever is available. The fix is a recv_exact loop. The same bug also affects `sock.recv(n)` for the body.

options.text: The sender's Nagle algorithm drops the header
options.explanation: Nagle may delay or coalesce data, but it never drops bytes.

options.text: recv() must always be called with a buffer of at least 4,096 bytes
options.explanation: A positive receive size smaller than 4,096 is valid. The bug is assuming the result always fills the requested length.

questions.workedExample:
1. `recv(4)` means 'give me **at most** 4 bytes'.
2. A local test may happen to return the complete header, but short reads are possible even on localhost.
3. Over a real network, the 4-byte header may straddle two segments, or the peer may write it in pieces. Then `recv(4)` returns, say, 2 bytes, and `unpack` fails.
4. `recv(n)` for the body has the same flaw, but fails silently by returning a short body.
5. Fix: use the lesson’s recv_exact and MAX_MSG, handling EOF/errors and bounding the decoded size before reading the body.

```python
hdr = recv_exact(sock, 4)
(n,) = struct.unpack("!I", hdr)
if n > MAX_MSG:
    raise ValueError("too large")
body = recv_exact(sock, n)
```

questions.prompt: On a POSIX system, diagnostics show that retained TIME_WAIT connections prevent an immediate listener rebind, with no competing listener. Which option should a restartable server configure before bind(), subject to that platform’s old/new socket reuse rules?

options.text: The old process is still running; kill it with kill -9
options.explanation: The question says nothing is listening. The port is held by connection state, not by a process.

options.text: Port 8080 is reserved for root; run the server as root
options.explanation: This is an address-reuse problem, not a permission error. Privileged-port thresholds are platform/configuration-dependent.

options.text: SO_REUSEADDR; Python socket.create_server enables it on POSIX
options.explanation: Correct. Configure appropriate reuse before binding. On Linux the relevant reuse case generally requires it on both the old and new sockets; exact rules differ across systems.

options.text: The ephemeral port range has been exhausted
options.explanation: Exhaustion of automatically selected local ports is a different failure mode. Here the supplied diagnostics identify retained TIME_WAIT state affecting an explicit bind; an existing conflicting allocation can also matter when a chosen fixed port overlaps the automatic range.

questions.workedExample:
TIME_WAIT retains TCP state after orderly closure and can affect rebinding. SO_REUSEADDR relaxes relevant address-reuse checks, subject to platform rules; it does not permit arbitrary sharing with an active listener. Set it before bind(), and configure the original listener appropriately too.

```python
s = socket.socket()
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET,
             socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 8080))
```

The caller must close s when finished. Port reuse does not mean new connections necessarily have different tuples; TCP’s retained state and sequence rules still matter.

questions.prompt:
Using the lesson's `recv_msg`, a peer sends these 10 bytes in one segment:

```
00 00 00 03 61 62 63 64 65 66
```

(0x61 to 0x66 are `a` to `f`.) What does the first `recv_msg(sock)` call return?

options.text: `b"abcdef"`
options.explanation: The header says the body is 3 bytes. recv_exact asks for exactly 3, so the last three stay in the buffer for the next call.

options.text: `b"abc"`
options.explanation: Correct. The header 00 00 00 03 decodes as 3, so recv_exact(sock, 3) returns b"abc". The bytes def remain unread.

options.text: `b"\x00\x00\x00\x03abcdef"`
options.explanation: recv_msg strips the 4-byte header and uses it as a length; it doesn't return it.

options.text: It raises EOFError because the message is incomplete
options.explanation: The 3-byte body is complete. EOFError only occurs if the peer closes before enough bytes arrive.

questions.workedExample:
1. `recv_exact(sock, 4)` reads `00 00 00 03`.
2. `struct.unpack("!I", ...)` reads a big-endian 32-bit unsigned integer: 3.
3. `recv_exact(sock, 3)` reads `61 62 63` = `b"abc"`.
4. `64 65 66` (`def`) remains in the socket buffer. The **next** `recv_msg` would take those three bytes plus one more as its header: an incomplete next header. It could be malformed input or part of a later message; the three bytes alone do not prove the peer uses another protocol. The lesson’s size limit rejects an oversized decoded next length.

questions.prompt: A thread-per-connection Python server handles 50 clients well. You need to hold 50,000 mostly idle WebSocket-style connections. Why is the threaded design likely to struggle, and what's the standard alternative?

options.text: Python threads can't call recv(); use processes instead
options.explanation: Threads can call recv(); in CPython’s usual GIL-enabled build, blocking socket I/O releases the GIL. Replacing each native thread with a process adds separate process-management costs and does not remove the need to measure resource limits.

options.text: TCP limits a server to 65,535 connections per port
options.explanation: A listener can serve more than 65,535 connections when peer endpoint tuples differ sufficiently. Resource and tuple limits still apply.

options.text: Each thread needs its own listening port
options.explanation: All connections are accepted from one listening socket; each thread only uses its accepted socket.

options.text: Native threads have stack and scheduling costs; a multiplexed runtime can serve many idle sockets with fewer threads
options.explanation: Correct. Backend and runtime details vary; a benchmark and resource limits determine actual capacity.

questions.workedExample: One native thread per connection adds stack reservations, task limits and scheduling overhead. A readiness or completion-based runtime can multiplex many waiting operations onto fewer threads. Connections still consume kernel buffers, application state, descriptors and runtime tasks. No fixed 50,000-connection capacity follows from choosing an event loop.

questions.prompt: A Linux service shows rising TcpExtListenOverflows and occasional delayed connection setup or first requests. With tcp_abort_on_overflow = 0, which explanation is consistent with these observations and should be investigated using captures and queue measurements?

options.text: The accept queue is overloaded; some handshakes may be deferred or dropped while the listener catches up
options.explanation: Correct. One overflow path ignores the final ACK and can recover after SYN+ACK retransmission. Other paths and causes exist; this counter alone does not prove that exact trace.

options.text: A SYN flood is filling the SYN queue
options.explanation: A SYN-queue problem alone is not established by this accept-overflow counter. Attack traffic can still contribute to several types of overload, so do not exclude it solely from one counter.

options.text: Nagle's algorithm is delaying the first request
options.explanation: Nagle is not the mechanism counted by a listen-queue overflow counter. Its delay is not universally bounded to a fixed millisecond range.

options.text: TIME_WAIT sockets are blocking new connections
options.explanation: TIME_WAIT on the server's port doesn't block new connections from different client tuples, and isn't counted by ListenOverflows.

questions.workedExample: Inspect backlog limits, arrival bursts, acceptance rate, blocked workers and resource limits. Linux can ignore a final ACK on an overflow path when abort-on-overflow is disabled, while the client already believes setup succeeded. Retries can then add delay, but exact timing and behaviour require capture/configuration evidence. A larger backlog absorbs some bursts; it does not fix sustained service-capacity shortfalls.

questions.prompt: Consider the lesson's `selectors` echo server, which calls `s.send(data)` once on a non-blocking socket. A client sends a lot of data quickly but reads its replies very slowly. Which problems can occur? Select all that apply.

options.text: send() may accept only part of `data`, and the rest is silently lost from the echo
options.explanation: Correct. A non-blocking send() returns how many bytes it took; the code ignores the return value, so any remainder is never sent.

options.text: send() may raise BlockingIOError when the socket's send buffer is completely full
options.explanation: Correct. Once the slow client's receive window and our send buffer are full, a non-blocking send can't accept anything, and the code doesn't catch it, so the loop crashes.

options.text: The non-blocking send call itself waits for the slow client to read
options.explanation: False. It returns a count or an error rather than waiting for writability. However, an unhandled exception can terminate this toy loop and interrupt service for every client.

options.text: Correct handling needs retained unsent output and write readiness, plus queue bounds, read backpressure and error handling
options.explanation: Correct. Account for partial writes and handle would-block, disconnection and cleanup; an unbounded output buffer merely moves the resource problem.

options.text: Switching to sendall() on the non-blocking socket fully solves it
options.explanation: On a non-blocking socket, sendall() can still raise BlockingIOError partway through, leaving an unknown amount sent. It doesn't replace proper output buffering.

questions.workedExample: The deliberately faulty loop ignores send()’s partial count and does not handle would-block. It can lose bytes or terminate. A non-blocking call does not wait for the slow peer, but loop termination affects all clients. Retain pending output, register write interest only while needed, bound queues and stop reading when output pressure is high. Handle stale readiness for accept/read/write and flush pending output on input half-close. sendall() alone does not solve non-blocking buffering.

questions.prompt: In the asyncio echo example, suppose the peer keeps uploading but never reads responses. With no output-size policy or total deadline added, what risk is introduced by deleting await writer.drain()?

options.text: Nothing; asyncio writes everything immediately
options.explanation: write() may send immediately or buffer unsent data. It does not wait for the receiving application to consume it.

options.text: The server crashes with BrokenPipeError immediately
options.explanation: Not reading replies does not itself require an immediate BrokenPipeError. Queued output can grow while the connection remains usable; independent failures or later endpoint closure are still possible.

options.text: TCP drops the responses, and the client receives them later via retransmission
options.explanation: Retransmission does not replace application backpressure. Data can accumulate in the asyncio transport’s output buffer.

options.text: Unsent output can grow excessively because the coroutine no longer waits for the transport’s backpressure
options.explanation: Correct. drain() waits when writing is paused at the high watermark until the buffer drains to the low watermark. Other failures or limits may stop growth; unlimited growth is a risk, not an inevitable trace.

questions.workedExample: If incoming data continues while output cannot drain, write() can accumulate unsent output in user space. drain() makes the coroutine cooperate with transport flow control, indirectly slowing further reads. Its watermarks concern the transport buffer, not a direct test for a zero TCP receive window. Removing it risks memory exhaustion; exact growth and termination depend on the runtime, peer and other limits.

questions.prompt: An Nginx-style server runs 8 worker processes. In design A they all accept from one shared listening socket. In design B each worker opens its own listening socket on port 443 with `SO_REUSEPORT`. What is the main effect of design B on Linux?

options.text: The kernel selects among separate eligible listening sockets, each with its own accept queue, which can reduce shared-listener contention
options.explanation: Correct. Linux’s default selection uses flow-related hashing, but optional BPF policies and implementation details vary. Neither perfect balancing nor removal of all locking is guaranteed.

options.text: It lets the server bind port 443 while old connections are in TIME_WAIT
options.explanation: That's what SO_REUSEADDR does. SO_REUSEPORT is about multiple simultaneous listeners.

options.text: Each worker receives a copy of every incoming connection
options.explanation: A connection is delivered to exactly one of the listening sockets; copying would make no sense for TCP.

options.text: It allows more than 65,535 connections to port 443
options.explanation: One listening socket can already have far more connections than that; connections are told apart by the client's address and port.

questions.workedExample: With one shared listener, workers take connections from one accept queue. An eligible SO_REUSEPORT group has separate listeners and queues; set the option before bind() and satisfy Linux’s effective-UID and binding requirements. Selection can distribute new connections without every worker sharing one accept queue. A stalled worker can still accumulate work, and measured workload balance is not guaranteed.
